method: Saute onion; add spices and saffron; stir 1 min.
Add all vegetables and chickpeas; cover with 1.5 litres water; simmer 30 min until all are tender.
Steam couscous above the broth if possible, adding butter and salt; fluff well.
Mound couscous on a wide platter; arrange vegetables on top.
Ladle broth over and serve the rest in a bowl on the side for people to add as they eat.

name: Mandazi (East African Doughnuts)
blurb: Lightly sweet, fluffy triangular doughnuts scented with cardamom and coconut — the classic East African tea-time bread, eaten from Mombasa to Nairobi.
tip: Rolling the dough on the thicker side (1cm) gives mandazi the soft, pillowy interior that distinguishes them from a flat, tough fry-bread.
method: Combine flour, sugar and cardamom; whisk egg into coconut milk; mix into dry ingredients to form a soft dough.
Knead briefly; rest 15 min; roll to 1cm thickness.
Cut into triangles or circles.
Deep fry at 170°C in batches until puffed and golden — 3-4 min each side.
Drain on paper; eat warm with tea.

name: Chapati with Spiced Beans
blurb: Soft, layered East African chapati alongside a tumble of spiced kidney beans — a filling, affordable breakfast found from Uganda to Tanzania.
tip: The log-coiling technique is what gives East African chapati its flaky, multi-layered texture distinct from a simple flatbread.
ingredients: Warm water to make a soft dough
For beans: 1 can kidney beans, 1 onion, 2 tomatoes, 1 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp turmeric, coriander
method: Make chapati: mix flour and salt; add water and knead 5 min; rest 15 min.
Roll a ball thin; brush oil; roll up into a log; coil the log; flatten again — this creates layers.
Cook on a dry pan 2 min each side until flecked with brown.
For beans: fry onion; add tomatoes, cumin, turmeric; cook 10 min; add beans; simmer 10 min; scatter coriander.
Serve folded chapati with beans alongside.

name: Uji (Fermented Grain Porridge)
blurb: A thin, lightly sour porridge of fermented maize or millet flour — Kenya and Tanzania's traditional morning drink, energising and easy to digest.
tip: Mix the flour with cold water first before adding to hot water — adding it dry creates lumps that are almost impossible to smooth out.
ingredients: 1 cup fermented maize or millet flour (or regular flour with 1 tbsp yoghurt for tang)
method: Mix flour to a smooth paste with 1 cup cold water; no lumps.
Bring remaining 3 cups water to a boil with salt.
Whisk in flour paste gradually, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Simmer on low heat 8-10 min, stirring frequently, until it thickens slightly and the raw flour taste disappears.
Sweeten; add lemon juice; serve warm in a cup or bowl; stir in milk if desired.

name: Injera with Teff Porridge (Genfo)
blurb: Thick Ethiopian teff flour porridge (genfo) served with a well of spiced butter and berbere chilli — a warming, nourishing highland breakfast.
tip: Cook genfo until it is genuinely thick and pulls from the sides — undercooked genfo is gluey and raw-tasting.
ingredients: 2 tbsp spiced Ethiopian butter (niter kibbeh) or plain butter
method: Bring water to a boil; gradually whisk in teff flour, stirring constantly.
Cook on low heat 10-15 min, stirring frequently with a wooden paddle, until very thick and pulling away from the sides.
The texture should be like very stiff polenta.
Mound into a bowl; make a well in the centre; spoon butter into the well; dust berbere over the butter.
Serve with plain yoghurt on the side to balance the heat.

name: Timatim Salad (Ethiopian Tomato Salad)
blurb: A refreshing Ethiopian salad of ripe tomatoes, red onion, jalapeño and coriander dressed with oil and lemon — simple, fresh and essential alongside injera.
tip: Draining the tomatoes briefly prevents the salad from becoming watery in the serving bowl — especially important if it sits for more than a few minutes.
method: Dice tomatoes and drain briefly in a colander to remove excess juice.
Combine tomatoes with onion, jalapeño and coriander.
Dress with olive oil, lemon juice, salt and pepper.
Toss gently; taste and adjust.
Serve immediately alongside injera or rice — it is a condiment as much as a salad.

name: Ugali with Sukuma Wiki
blurb: Kenya's national dish — a dense, stiff maize porridge (ugali) served with braised collard greens (sukuma wiki) — the everyday meal of millions.
tip: Ugali should hold a firm shape when scooped — if it flows or sags, cook longer; the correct texture lets you roll a ball without sticking to your palm.
ingredients: 2 cups maize flour (ugali flour or fine polenta)
For sukuma wiki: 1 large bunch collard greens, shredded
method: Bring water and salt to a boil; gradually pour in maize flour, stirring vigorously.
Cook on low heat 15-20 min, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, until it pulls from the sides and holds its shape.
For sukuma: saute onion in oil; add tomatoes and cumin; cook 5 min; add greens and a splash of water; cook 8 min.
Shape ugali into a dome on a plate or board.
Serve sukuma alongside — tear and scoop the ugali with your right hand.

name: Githeri (Maize and Bean Stew)
blurb: Kenya's ancestral dish of boiled maize and kidney beans slow-simmered with onion, tomato and spices — humble, nourishing and deeply comforting.
tip: The beans and maize should be fully cooked separately before combining — trying to cook them together from raw results in uneven textures.
ingredients: 1 cup dried kidney beans, soaked and cooked
1 cup dried maize or canned hominy
method: Saute onion in oil until golden; add carrot and cook 3 min.
Add tomatoes, curry powder and cumin; cook 5 min.
Add cooked beans and maize; stir to combine.
Add 1 cup water; simmer 25 min until thick and stew-like.
Season; scatter coriander; serve with ugali or chapati.

name: Red Lentil and Vegetable Stew (Misir Wat)
blurb: Ethiopian berbere-spiced red lentil stew — a pillar of the injera plate, deeply flavoured and deeply satisfying in its simplicity.
tip: Dry-caramelising the onion without oil is the defining technique of misir wat — it builds a depth of flavour that oil-fried onion cannot replicate.
ingredients: 2 tbsp niter kibbeh (spiced butter) or plain butter
method: Dry-fry onion on low heat without oil for 15 min, stirring, until very dark and caramelised — this is the key step.
Add spiced butter, garlic, ginger and berbere; fry 2 min.
Add lentils and water; bring to a boil; simmer 15-20 min until lentils are fully dissolved.
Stir well — the stew should be thick and almost spreadable.
Serve on injera or rice.

name: Irio (Kenyan Mashed Peas and Corn)
blurb: A Kikuyu staple of mashed potato, peas and corn blended together — dense, green-flecked and deeply comforting, often served with a side stew.
tip: Do not over-mash irio — the chunky texture with visible pieces of pea and corn is what makes it irio rather than plain mashed potato.
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
method: Boil potatoes in salted water until very tender; add peas and corn last 5 min.
Drain, reserving a cup of cooking water.
Mash roughly with butter, adding cooking water to reach a thick, chunky texture.
The peas should turn the mash slightly green — this is characteristic.
Season well; serve mounded as a side to stews or grilled vegetables.

name: Vegetable Pilau (East African)
blurb: Basmati rice cooked with whole spices, onion and mixed vegetables — the celebratory rice of the East African coast, perfumed with cinnamon and cardamom.
tip: Deeply golden onions (almost burnt) are the authentic flavour base of East African pilau — pale onions produce a bland, flat-tasting dish.
method: Fry onion in oil until deeply golden; add garlic, ginger and whole spices; fry 1 min.
Add pilau masala; fry 30 seconds; add potato and carrot.
Pour in stock and bring to a boil; add rice, peas and salt.
Cover tightly; cook on the lowest heat 15 min; do not lift the lid.
Rest 5 min; fluff gently; serve with kachumbari on the side.

name: Kachumbari (East African Fresh Salad)
blurb: Diced tomato, red onion and coriander in a sharp lime dressing — the ubiquitous East African fresh salad that accompanies almost every meal.
tip: Rinsing the raw onion under cold water removes the harsh sulfur compounds and makes the flavour clean and mild without losing the crunch.
method: Dice tomatoes; dice onion small — rinse diced onion in cold water and squeeze dry to mellow its sharpness.
Combine tomato, cucumber, onion, chilli and coriander.
Dress with lime juice, olive oil, salt and pepper.
Taste; adjust lime and salt.
Serve immediately — it is at its best fresh.

name: East African Samosa
blurb: Crisp, golden pastry triangles filled with a spiced potato and pea mixture — the East African samosa, found at every tea stall from Nairobi to Dar es Salaam.
tip: A stiff pastry dough (less water) is essential — too soft and the samosa will burst in the oil; too thick and it stays pale and doughy inside.
ingredients: For pastry: 2 cups flour, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp oil, warm water to bind
For filling: 3 potatoes (boiled and diced), 1/2 cup peas, 1 onion (finely diced), 1 tsp curry powder, 1/2 tsp cumin, salt, fresh coriander
method: Make pastry: mix flour, salt and oil; add warm water to form a stiff, smooth dough; rest 20 min.
Fry onion; add spices; add potato and peas; cook 3 min; season; cool.
Roll pastry thin; cut into strips; fold each strip into a cone; fill; seal the top.
Deep fry at 175°C until golden — 3-4 min.
Drain; serve hot with tamarind chutney.

name: Mahamri (Swahili Coconut Doughnut)
blurb: Slightly sweet, yeasted coconut milk doughnuts from the Swahili coast — softer and richer than mandazi, with a characteristic diamond shape.
tip: Mahamri must fry at a lower temperature than mandazi — the higher sugar content burns quickly on high heat before the interior is cooked.
method: Combine flour, yeast, sugar and cardamom; add coconut milk and enough warm water to form a soft dough.
Knead until smooth; rest 1 hour until puffy.
Roll to 1cm thickness; cut into diamond shapes.
Fry at 165°C until golden and cooked through — 4-5 min each side on low heat.
Drain; eat warm with tea.

name: Viazi Karai (Spiced Fried Potato)
blurb: Potato chunks dipped in a spiced gram flour batter and deep fried until golden — a Zanzibari street food eaten with tamarind chutney.
tip: Boil the potatoes through before battering — raw potato inside a cooked batter is the most common mistake with viazi karai.
ingredients: For batter: 1 cup gram flour (chickpea flour), 1 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 1/2 tsp chilli powder, salt, water to form a thick batter
Tamarind chutney and lime to serve
method: Mix gram flour with spices and enough water to make a thick, coating batter.
Dip boiled potato pieces in batter to coat fully.
Deep fry at 175°C until the batter is golden and crisp — 3-4 min.
Drain on paper; serve immediately — they lose their crispness quickly.
Squeeze lime; serve with tamarind chutney.

name: Bhajia (Kenyan Potato Bhajia)
blurb: Thin slices of potato coated in a spiced gram flour batter and fried crisp — the Kenyan coastal bhajia, lighter and more delicate than the Indian version.
tip: Thin, even potato slices — use a mandoline if you have one — are what give Kenyan bhajia their characteristic delicacy.
method: Combine gram flour, spices, coriander and salt; whisk in water until a thin, coating batter forms.
Dip each potato slice; allow excess to drip off.
Fry in hot oil at 175°C in small batches until golden and crisp — 2-3 min.
Do not overcrowd the pan — bhajia must float freely to crisp evenly.
Drain; serve hot with green chutney.

name: Açaí Bowl
blurb: A Brazilian icon — frozen açaí blended thick and topped with granola, banana, honey and coconut — the Amazon in a bowl.
tip: Keep the liquid to an absolute minimum — an açaí bowl should be thick enough to support toppings, not a smoothie that soaks them.
ingredients: Toppings: 3 tbsp granola, 1/2 banana sliced, 1 tbsp honey, 1 tbsp shredded coconut, fresh berries, 1 tsp chia seeds
method: Blend frozen açaí pulp with frozen banana and milk — start with minimum liquid to keep thick.
Blend until smooth but still thick enough to eat with a spoon; it should not pour.
Pour into a chilled bowl.
Arrange toppings in rows: granola, banana, berries, coconut, chia.
Drizzle honey; serve immediately before it melts.

name: Tapioca Crepe with Coconut and Banana
blurb: Gluten-free tapioca starch crepes with a sweet coconut and banana filling — Brazil's north-eastern tapioca, unique and simple.
tip: Tapioca crepes set and stiffen within seconds of being removed from the pan — fill and fold while still in the pan over heat.
method: Hydrate tapioca starch with a little water until it holds when squeezed; it should be crumbly but moist.
Press through a fine sieve to form a dry, even layer in a non-stick pan over medium heat.
Cook 2 min until the surface sets and the edges begin to lift; flip carefully.
Immediately lay banana and coconut on one half; fold over.
Drizzle honey; eat while the outside is still crisp.

name: Changua (Colombian Milk Soup with Egg)
blurb: A Colombian Andean highland soup of warm milk, poached egg and stale bread — the gentle, warming breakfast of Bogotá and the surrounding highlands.
tip: A gentle simmer — not a boil — keeps the egg white tender; a rolling boil shreds the white before it sets.
ingredients: 2 slices stale bread or toast, cubed
method: Bring milk and water to a gentle simmer with spring onion, salt and a little butter.
Crack eggs directly into the simmering milk; poach 4-5 min until whites are set.
Place cubed bread in the bottom of each bowl.
Carefully ladle the milk soup and an egg into each bowl.
Scatter coriander; add more spring onion; serve with extra toast.

name: Calentado (Colombian Leftover Breakfast)
blurb: Leftover rice and red beans fried with egg and plantain — the beloved Colombian Monday morning breakfast built from Sunday's supper.
tip: The slight crisping of the rice and beans in the pan — not just reheating — is what makes calentado a proper dish rather than warmed leftovers.
ingredients: 1 cup cooked red beans with their sauce
method: Fry plantain slices in oil until golden on both sides; set aside.
In the same pan, fry rice and beans together, tossing until heated through and slightly crisped.
Push to one side; fry eggs sunny side up in the same pan.
Plate rice-and-beans; add egg on top; arrange plantain alongside.
Scatter coriander; add hot sauce.

name: Locro de Papa (Ecuadorian Potato Soup)
blurb: A thick, milky Ecuadorian potato soup made creamy with melted white cheese and finished with avocado — the Andean highlands in a bowl.
tip: The cheese should melt softly into the broth, not fully dissolve — semi-firm white cheese (not mature cheddar) is what achieves this.
ingredients: Avocado slices and coriander to serve
method: Saute onion with achiote in oil until orange and fragrant; add garlic.
Add potato and stock; simmer 20 min until potato is very soft.
Mash some potato directly in the pot to thicken; add milk and stir.
Add cubed cheese; stir gently — it should melt into creamy pockets.
Ladle into bowls; top with avocado and coriander; serve with bread.

name: Sopa de Quinoa (Andean Quinoa Soup)
blurb: Quinoa simmered in a vegetable broth with potato, carrot and Andean herbs — the ancient grain of the Incas in its most traditional soup form.
tip: Quinoa must be thoroughly rinsed before cooking to remove saponins — without rinsing the soup will have a bitter, soapy edge.
ingredients: Salt, pepper and lime to serve
method: Saute onion and garlic in oil; add cumin; cook 1 min.
Add carrot, celery and potato; stir.
Add stock; bring to a boil; add rinsed quinoa.
Simmer 20 min until quinoa is cooked (white tails will have unfurled) and potato is tender.
Season; scatter herbs; squeeze lime; serve hot.

name: Causa Limeña (Peruvian Potato Terrine)
blurb: Cold, layered potato terrine filled with avocado and vegetables — Lima's most elegant street food, as beautiful to look at as it is to eat.
tip: The potato must be mashed while hot and mixed with oil while warm — cold potato mixed with oil turns grainy and will not hold together.
ingredients: 4 yellow potatoes, boiled and mashed hot
2 tbsp aji amarillo paste (or 1 tbsp mild chilli paste)
method: Mix hot mashed potato with aji amarillo, lime juice, oil and salt until smooth and bright yellow; cool to room temperature.
Season avocado and tomato separately with lime, salt and pepper.
Press half the potato into a rectangular mould or loaf tin; layer avocado and tomato on top; press remaining potato over to cover.
Refrigerate 30 min to firm.
Unmould; slice and serve cold garnished with olives and boiled egg.

name: Chupe de Verduras (Andean Vegetable Chowder)
blurb: A rich Andean vegetable and quinoa chowder with milk and fresh cheese — the warming soup of the highlands, thickened with potato and brightened with fresh herbs.
tip: Add milk and cheese off or on lowest heat only — boiling after adding dairy splits the milk and makes the chowder grainy.
ingredients: 1 ear of corn, kernels cut off
method: Saute onion and garlic; add cumin; add potato and stock; simmer 10 min.
Add quinoa, courgette and corn; simmer 15 min until quinoa is cooked.
Stir in milk; bring gently to a simmer; add cheese; stir until just melted.
Season; taste; adjust.
Serve in deep bowls; scatter fresh mint and coriander on top.

name: Tofu Picante Salteado (Spicy Stir-Fried Tofu)
blurb: Tofu and vegetables stir-fried in the Peruvian lomo saltado style — soy sauce, tomatoes and aji amarillo over white rice and chips.
tip: Lomo saltado is a high-heat, quick-cook dish — a pan that is not ripping hot will steam the ingredients rather than char them.
ingredients: Steamed rice and fries to serve
method: Press tofu; cut into cubes; fry in hot oil until golden on all sides; remove.
In the same pan on very high heat, fry onion and garlic 1 min — the pan must be smoking.
Add tomatoes; toss 1 min.
Add soy sauce, aji amarillo and cumin; toss; return tofu.
Serve immediately over rice; add fries; scatter coriander; squeeze lime.

name: Aji de Verduras (Vegetable Aji Stew)
blurb: Yellow potato and mixed vegetables simmered in a creamy aji amarillo and bread-thickened sauce — a vegetarian adaptation of Peru's iconic aji de gallina.
tip: Soaking the bread in milk before blending is what gives aji sauce its characteristic thick, creamy, velvety body.
ingredients: For sauce: 3 aji amarillo chillies (or paste), 2 slices white bread (soaked in milk), 1 onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1/4 cup walnuts, 1/2 cup milk
Parmesan and black olives to garnish
method: Blend soaked bread, aji amarillo, walnuts, garlic and milk until smooth.
Fry onion in oil until soft; add blended sauce; stir and cook 5 min.
Add courgettes and carrot; cook 8 min.
Add boiled potato halves; coat everything in the sauce; simmer 5 min more.
Serve garnished with parmesan, olives and egg.

name: Sopa Paraguaya (Cornbread Casserole)
blurb: Despite its name ('Paraguayan soup') this is a dense, moist cornbread baked with cheese and onion — Paraguay's national dish and a staple at every meal.
tip: Sopa paraguaya is done when a skewer comes out clean and the top is uniformly golden — an underbaked sopa will collapse when cut.
ingredients: 1 cup cottage cheese or fresh white cheese
method: Saute onion in oil until soft and translucent; cool.
Beat eggs; mix with milk, oil, cottage cheese and salt.
Stir in cornmeal and baking powder; fold in sauteed onion.
Pour into a greased baking dish — batter should be thick.
Bake at 190°C for 35-40 min until set in the centre and golden on top.

name: Tequeños (Venezuelan Cheese Bread Sticks)
blurb: Twisted dough sticks wrapped around stretchy white cheese and fried golden — Venezuela's most beloved party snack, impossible to stop at one.
tip: Serve tequeños immediately — they are at their peak for about 4 minutes while the cheese is still liquid inside the crisp crust.
ingredients: 200g queso blanco or mozzarella, cut into sticks
method: Rub butter into flour with salt and sugar until crumbly; add egg and water; mix to a dough; chill 15 min.
Roll out thin; cut into strips.
Wrap a strip tightly around each cheese stick, overlapping as you go; press ends to seal.
Deep fry at 175°C until golden — 3-4 min; do not overcook or cheese escapes.
Drain briefly; serve immediately while the cheese is still molten.

name: Patacones (Twice-Fried Plantain)
blurb: Green plantain rounds fried, smashed flat and fried again until crispy — Colombia and Ecuador's most addictive snack, eaten with everything.
tip: Smash the plantains while still warm from the first fry — cold plantain cracks and shatters rather than pressing flat.
ingredients: 2 green (unripe) plantains, peeled and sliced into 2cm rounds
Guacamole or hogao (Colombian tomato sauce) to serve
method: Fry plantain rounds at 160°C for 4-5 min until cooked through but not coloured; drain.
While warm, smash each piece flat with a flat-bottomed glass or a tostonera.
Fry a second time at 185°C for 2-3 min until deeply golden and crisp.
Drain; salt immediately.
Serve with guacamole or hogao.

name: Salteñas de Queso (Bolivian Cheese Pastries)
blurb: Bolivian baked empanada-style pastries with a slightly sweet, juicy cheese and vegetable filling — the morning street food of La Paz.
tip: The gelled filling is the secret to juicy salteñas — liquid filling at assembly time will leak; it must be solid cold and liquefy in the oven.
ingredients: For dough: 3 cups flour, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsp sugar, 100g butter, 2 eggs, 4 tbsp water
For filling: 200g white cheese (cubed), 1 potato (boiled and diced), 1/2 cup green olives, 2 tbsp parsley, 1 tsp aji amarillo paste, salt, gelatin stock to set (2 tbsp gelatin in 1 cup stock, cooled)
method: Make dough: rub butter into flour with salt and sugar; bind with egg and water; chill 30 min.
Mix cheese, potato, olives, parsley and aji paste into the cooled gelatin stock; chill until gelled — this creates a juicy filling.
Roll dough thin; cut circles; fill each with 2 tbsp filling; crimp edges shut.
Brush with egg wash; bake at 220°C for 20-25 min until deeply golden.
Eat while hot — the filling liquefies as it bakes.

name: Koko (Spiced Millet Porridge)
blurb: A Ghanaian and Burkinabé fermented millet porridge spiced with ginger and cloves — the warming breakfast sold by roadside vendors across West Africa at dawn.
tip: Millet porridge thickens dramatically as it cools — serve immediately or keep over very low heat, adding water as needed.
ingredients: 1 cup millet flour (or fermented millet for authenticity)
Koose (black-eyed pea fritters) to serve alongside
method: Mix millet flour to a smooth paste with 1 cup cold water.
Bring remaining 3 cups water to a boil.
Slowly whisk in the millet paste; stir constantly to prevent lumps.
Add ginger, cloves, pepper and salt; cook on medium-low heat 15 min, stirring frequently.
Sweeten; serve warm in bowls — eat with koose for the full street-food experience.

name: Tom Brown (Roasted Corn and Groundnut Porridge)
blurb: A Ghanaian porridge of roasted and ground corn and groundnuts — rich, slightly smoky and deeply nourishing, often a child's first solid food.
tip: Whisking the paste into boiling water rather than adding cold water to cold paste gives a smoother, lump-free porridge every time.
ingredients: 1 cup tom brown powder (or roast equal parts corn flour and ground peanuts in a dry pan)
method: If making from scratch: dry-roast corn flour and ground peanuts separately until golden; combine equal parts.
Mix tom brown powder with 1 cup cold water to a smooth paste.
Bring 3 cups water to a boil; whisk in paste; stir constantly.
Cook 10-12 min on low heat, stirring, until thick and fully cooked.
Sweeten; add ginger; stir in milk if using; serve warm.

name: Masa (Fermented Rice Cakes)
blurb: Fluffy Nigerian fermented rice cakes cooked in a special pan — eaten sweet with honey or savoury with pepper soup, they are the Northern Nigerian breakfast.
tip: A takoyaki or aebleskiver pan creates the authentic round shape — without a dedicated pan, pour batter into oiled rings on a griddle instead.
ingredients: Oil for the masa pan or a takoyaki/aebleskiver pan
method: Soak raw rice overnight; blend with cooked rice, yeast, sugar, salt and enough water to form a thick pancake batter; ferment 4-6 hours.
Heat masa pan; grease each well generously.
Pour batter into each well; cook 3-4 min covered until the surface sets.
Flip each cake; cook 2 min on the other side.
Serve warm with honey, sugar or a side of pepper soup.

name: Koose (Black-Eyed Pea Fritter)
blurb: Fluffy, airy fritters of soaked and ground black-eyed peas spiced with pepper — Ghana's breakfast fritter, fried in small rounds and eaten with koko.
tip: Beating the batter vigorously before frying is the step that makes koose light and airy inside rather than dense and doughy.
ingredients: 1 cup dried black-eyed peas, soaked overnight
1-2 Scotch bonnet or habanero chillies (to taste)
method: Drain soaked peas; rub vigorously between your palms to remove the skins; rinse away skins.
Blend deskinned peas with onion, chilli and salt using minimal water to a thick, fluffy paste.
Beat the paste vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3 min — this incorporates air.
Drop by tablespoon into hot oil; fry at 175°C until golden — 3-4 min.
Drain; serve hot alongside koko or tea.

name: Waakye (Rice and Beans in Sorghum Leaves)
blurb: Ghanaian rice and black-eyed peas cooked together with dried sorghum leaves — which turn everything a deep reddish-brown — eaten with a feast of toppings.
tip: The sorghum leaves are purely for colour and a subtle earthy flavour — if unavailable, a few dried red beans will tint the rice a similar reddish hue.
ingredients: 2-3 dried sorghum or millet leaves (for colour) or 1 tsp black food colouring
Toppings: gari (cassava granules), shito (black pepper sauce), boiled egg, fried plantain, avocado
method: Boil black-eyed peas with sorghum leaves for 20 min; remove leaves.
Add rice; add water to cover 3cm above; salt; cook 20 min until both are fully tender and a brownish-red colour.
Meanwhile prepare toppings: fry plantain; boil eggs; warm shito sauce.
Pile waakye on a banana leaf or plate.
Add toppings to taste — the more varied, the better.

name: Kontomire Stew (Cocoyam Leaf Stew)
blurb: A Ghanaian stew of cocoyam leaves (or spinach) cooked in palmnut cream with smoked spices and served over boiled yam — a deeply flavoured, nutritious staple.
tip: Cocoyam leaves must be very finely chopped and cooked thoroughly — under-cooked leaves have an itchy texture from their oxalate content.
ingredients: 300g cocoyam leaves or spinach, finely chopped
1 cup palmnut cream (or red palm oil broth)
Boiled yam or plantain to serve
method: Blend tomatoes, onion, garlic and Scotch bonnet.
Heat palmnut cream; fry blended paste 8 min until oil rises.
Add finely chopped cocoyam leaves; stir; cook 10 min.
Add crayfish if using; season with salt.
Serve over boiled yam slices or with plantain.

name: Vegetable Groundnut Soup
blurb: A rich West African peanut soup with tomatoes, mixed vegetables and warming spices — thick, hearty and complex, served over rice or with fufu.
tip: Whisk the peanut butter with warm stock first to form a smooth paste before adding to the pot — cold peanut butter added directly will lump.
ingredients: 2 cups mixed vegetables (aubergine, spinach, sweet potato)
method: Fry onion and garlic; add tomatoes and Scotch bonnet; cook 8 min.
Whisk peanut butter into 1 cup warm stock until smooth; add to the pot.
Add remaining stock, ginger and all vegetables; stir; bring to a boil.
Simmer 20-25 min until vegetables are tender and soup is thick.
Season; serve over rice or with fufu.

name: Okra Stew with Yam
blurb: Sliced okra simmered in a tomato and pepper base to a thick, silky stew — eaten with boiled yam or pounded yam, a beloved comfort of the Nigerian kitchen.
tip: Slice okra thinly (3-4mm) and do not overcook — the goal is a silky, slightly gelatinous stew, not a brown mush.
ingredients: 3 tbsp red palm oil or vegetable oil
Boiled or pounded yam to serve
method: Heat palm oil; fry onion until softened; add garlic and Scotch bonnet; fry 1 min.
Add blended tomato; cook 10 min until thick and oil rises.
Add sliced okra and crayfish if using; stir gently.
Cook 8-10 min — the okra will release its natural thickener and the stew will become silky.
Season; serve with boiled yam.

name: Bambara Groundnut Stew
blurb: A West African peanut and bean stew from the Sahel — nutty, tomato-based and filling, eaten with rice across Mali, Senegal and Guinea.
tip: This stew thickens significantly on standing — add extra stock to loosen when reheating.
ingredients: 1 cup bambara groundnuts or black-eyed peas, cooked
method: Fry onion in palm oil; add garlic and Scotch bonnet; add tomatoes; cook 8 min.
Whisk peanut butter in warm stock until smooth; add to pot.
Add cooked beans, paprika and remaining stock; stir.
Simmer 25 min until thick and rich; adjust consistency.
Season; scatter coriander; serve over white rice.

name: Suya-Spiced Tofu with Yam
blurb: Firm tofu marinated in the smoky West African suya spice mix and grilled until charred, served with wedges of boiled yam — the plant-based suya experience.
tip: Pressing the tofu dry before marinating is essential — wet tofu will not form a proper crust and the spice paste will steam off rather than char.
ingredients: 300g firm tofu, pressed and sliced into steaks
For suya spice: 2 tbsp roasted groundnut powder, 1 tsp paprika, 1 tsp ginger, 1/2 tsp garlic powder, 1/2 tsp cayenne, 1/2 tsp onion powder, salt
Sliced onion and tomato to serve
method: Mix suya spice with oil to form a paste; press onto tofu steaks; marinate 15 min.
Grill or fry tofu in a hot, dry pan 4-5 min each side until deeply charred and crusted.
Boil yam until tender; slice.
Arrange tofu over yam slices.
Serve with raw onion rings and sliced tomato.

name: Plantain Stew with Black-Eyed Peas
blurb: Ripe plantain simmered with black-eyed peas in a tomato and palm oil sauce — a sweet, savoury and satisfying Ghanaian main course.
tip: Use ripe but not overripe plantain (yellow with black spots) — green plantain stays hard, while overripe plantain collapses completely into the sauce.
ingredients: 2 ripe plantains, peeled and cut into chunks
method: Heat palm oil; fry onion and garlic until soft; add blended tomato and Scotch bonnet; cook 10 min.
Add black-eyed peas and ground coriander; cook 5 min.
Add plantain chunks; stir gently — ripe plantain is delicate.
Add 1/2 cup water; cover and simmer 12-15 min until plantain is fully tender.
Season; scatter fresh coriander; serve with rice.

name: Eba with Vegetable Ofe Onugbu
blurb: Smooth cassava flour dough (eba) served with a bitter leaf vegetable soup thick with palm oil and spices — a quintessential Nigerian meal.
tip: Mix eba in a clean pot with a wooden spoon — it requires quick, vigorous stirring to prevent lumps and achieve the characteristic smooth, stretchy texture.
ingredients: 1 cup cassava flour (garri), yellow or white
For ofe onugbu: 1 bunch bitter leaf (washed) or spinach, 200g cocoyam powder (to thicken), palm oil, 1 onion, 2 stock cubes, Scotch bonnet, crayfish powder, salt
method: Boil 1 cup water per serving; pour garri in, stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon to form a smooth, stretchy dough; add more hot water if too stiff; rest 2 min.
For soup: heat palm oil; saute onion; add blended tomato and Scotch bonnet; cook 8 min.
Stir in dissolved cocoyam powder to thicken; add bitter leaf and crayfish; simmer 10 min.
Season; check thickness — ofe onugbu should coat a spoon.
Shape eba into a ball; serve with soup poured around.

name: Puff Puff (Nigerian Doughnuts)
blurb: Airy, yeasted Nigerian doughnuts that puff into rounds as they fry — the original West African street snack, perfectly simple.
tip: A full 45-minute rest is important — under-proofed puff puff will not be airy and will absorb more oil during frying.
method: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, nutmeg and salt; add warm water; mix to a smooth batter (thicker than pancake batter).
Cover and rest 45 min-1 hour until bubbly and slightly risen.
Heat oil to 175°C; use a wet hand or two spoons to drop balls of batter into the oil.
Fry 3-4 min, turning, until golden on all sides.
Drain on paper; dust with sugar if desired; eat warm.

name: Chin Chin
blurb: Deep-fried strips or knots of sweetened dough, crunchy throughout — Nigeria and Ghana's ubiquitous snack that keeps for weeks in a tin.
tip: Frying on lower heat for longer is the secret to chin chin that is crunchy all the way through rather than just on the outside.
method: Rub butter into flour until like breadcrumbs; stir in sugar, salt and nutmeg.
Beat egg with milk; add to flour mixture; mix to a stiff, smooth dough — add more milk if needed.
Roll thin (3-4mm); cut into small strips or knot shapes.
Deep fry at 160°C in batches until golden throughout — 5-6 min on low heat.
Drain fully; cool completely before storing — they crisp up as they cool.

name: Plantain Chips
blurb: Thinly sliced unripe plantain fried until wafer-crisp and salted — West Africa's original crisp, eaten from street stalls across the continent.
tip: Paper-thin slices are non-negotiable — thick slices take too long and cook unevenly, becoming oily in the centre before the surface crisps.
ingredients: Optional: chilli powder or suya spice for dusting
method: Slice plantains paper-thin on a mandoline or with a sharp knife; pat completely dry.
Fry in small batches at 175°C until golden and completely crisp — 2-3 min.
They should be rigid, not flexible, when done.
Drain immediately; salt while hot; dust with chilli if using.
Cool completely before packing — they become crispier as they cool.

name: Bofrot (Ghanaian Sweet Doughnuts)
blurb: Slightly sweet, coconut-scented Ghanaian doughnuts — denser and smaller than Nigerian puff puff, with a characteristic pale golden colour and smooth skin.
tip: Bofrot should be pale golden, not deeply brown — the coconut milk in the dough browns faster than a plain dough and over-browning turns them bitter.
method: Combine flour, sugar and yeast; add egg, coconut milk and enough warm water to form a soft, sticky dough.
Knead briefly; cover and prove 30-45 min until slightly risen.
Wet hands; shape into small balls (walnut-sized).
Fry at 165°C until pale golden — 4-5 min — turning frequently for even colour.
Drain; dust with icing sugar if desired.

name: Suya-Spiced Groundnuts
blurb: Peanuts tossed in a suya spice paste and roasted until fragrant and lightly crusted — the bar snack and roadside snack of Nigeria and beyond.
tip: Remove the peanuts from the oven when they smell toasted but still look lightly coloured — carryover heat will finish them and they burn quickly past this point.
ingredients: 2 tbsp groundnut powder (or fine peanut butter powder)
method: Mix all spices with oil and peanut powder to form a coating paste.
Toss raw peanuts in the paste until evenly coated.
Spread on a baking tray; roast at 180°C for 8-10 min, shaking halfway, until fragrant and lightly toasted.
Cool completely — they crisp and the spice sets as they cool.
Store in an airtight jar; they keep for one week.

name: Dhokla
blurb: Light, spongy steamed cakes made from fermented gram flour — Gujarat's beloved breakfast bite, tangy and cloud-soft.
tip: Add the Eno and pour into the steamer in one swift motion — any delay and the batter loses its rise.
ingredients: fresh coriander and grated coconut to garnish
method: Mix gram flour, yogurt, turmeric, ginger-chili paste, and salt into a smooth batter. Rest 30–60 min.
Grease a round tray. Add Eno to batter, stir quickly — batter will foam up.
Pour into tray immediately; steam 12–15 min until a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool 5 min, then cut into squares.
Heat oil, splutter mustard seeds, curry leaves, and chilies. Add sugar and water; pour over dhokla.
Garnish with coriander and coconut. Serve with green chutney.

name: Vegetable Uttapam
blurb: Thick, spongy dosa-style pancakes studded with colourful vegetables — a wholesome South Indian breakfast that is as pretty as it is filling.
tip: Use well-fermented batter — thin or under-fermented batter gives flat, dense uttapam rather than the characteristic spongy texture.
method: Heat a tawa on medium; grease lightly.
Pour a ladleful of batter; spread gently into a thick circle — do not thin like a dosa.
Scatter onion, tomato, chili, and coriander on top; press lightly.
Drizzle oil around edges; cook until base is golden and set.
Flip carefully; cook 2 min on the vegetable side.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.

name: Paneer Paratha
blurb: Whole-wheat flatbreads stuffed with spiced crumbled paneer — golden, crisp-edged, and utterly satisfying with a dollop of cold butter.
tip: Keep the filling dry — wet paneer tears the dough. Squeeze out any liquid from the paneer before mixing with spices.
method: Knead flour with salt and water into a smooth pliable dough. Rest 15 min.
Mix paneer with chili, cumin, red chili powder, coriander, and salt.
Divide dough into balls; roll each into a disc.
Place filling in centre, gather edges, seal, and roll gently into a flat round.
Cook on a hot tawa with ghee, pressing gently, until golden on both sides.
Serve hot with yogurt, pickle, and butter.

name: Ragi Dosa
blurb: Crispy, lacy dosas made from finger millet (ragi) and rice flour — a nutritious South Indian breakfast packed with calcium and fibre.
tip: Ragi batter does not spread as easily as plain dosa — pour from the centre and ease outward quickly before it sets.
method: Mix all flours with yogurt, cumin, chili, ginger, and salt.
Add water gradually to reach a thin pourable batter. Rest 10 min.
Heat a tawa on high; reduce to medium-high; grease lightly.
Pour a ladleful of batter from the edges inward, spreading as thin as possible.
Drizzle oil around edges; cook until crisp and lightly brown.
Fold and serve with coconut chutney.

name: Rava Idli
blurb: Soft, instant idlis made from tempered semolina — no overnight fermentation needed, making this the busy-morning hero of South Indian kitchens.
tip: The batter thickens as it rests — add a splash of water if needed before adding Eno, so idlis come out soft, not dense.
method: Heat oil; splutter mustard seeds, cashews, and curry leaves until cashews are golden.
Add semolina; roast on low 3–4 min until fragrant. Cool slightly.
Mix in yogurt, coriander, and salt; add water to get a thick batter.
Rest 10 min — rava absorbs liquid and thickens.
Add Eno; stir gently and spoon into greased idli moulds immediately.
Steam 10–12 min until set. Serve with sambar and coconut chutney.

name: Curd Rice
blurb: Creamy, cooling rice blended with yogurt and finished with a mustard-curry leaf temper — South India's beloved comfort dish and the traditional finale of a full meal.
tip: Use slightly warm rice — mixing yogurt into hot rice curdles it. If rice has cooled completely, a splash of milk brings the creaminess back.
ingredients: pomegranate seeds and fresh coriander to garnish
method: Cook rice until soft and slightly overcooked; mash lightly with a spoon while warm.
Cool to room temperature; mix in yogurt and milk until creamy. Season with salt.
Heat oil; splutter mustard seeds and urad dal until dal turns golden.
Add green chili, ginger, curry leaves, and red chili; fry 30 sec.
Pour tempering over rice and mix gently.
Garnish with pomegranate seeds and coriander; serve at room temperature or lightly chilled.

name: Paneer Butter Masala
blurb: Velvety, mildly spiced tomato-cream gravy cradling golden paneer cubes — the restaurant classic that has won hearts far beyond India.
tip: Blanching and pureeing the tomatoes gives a smoother, sweeter gravy — the skin and seeds are the source of any bitterness.
method: Heat oil; sauté onion puree until it leaves oil, about 10 min on medium.
Add ginger-garlic paste; cook 2 min. Add spices and cook 1 min.
Pour in tomato puree; simmer until thick and oil separates, 8–10 min.
Stir in butter and cream; simmer 2 min.
Add paneer cubes; fold gently and simmer 3 min.
Crush kasuri methi between palms; stir in. Garnish with coriander and a swirl of cream.

name: Jeera Rice
blurb: Fragrant basmati rice tempered with cumin in ghee — the simplest, most aromatic side that elevates any dal or curry.
tip: Soaking the rice shortens cooking time and keeps grains from sticking — each grain should be separate and elongated.
method: Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot; add cumin seeds and let sizzle until fragrant, about 30 sec.
Add rice; stir and coat with ghee for 1 min.
Pour in water and salt; bring to a boil.
Reduce heat to very low, cover tightly, and cook 12–15 min until water is absorbed.
Rest covered 5 min; fluff with a fork. Garnish with coriander.

name: Aloo Gobi
blurb: Potatoes and cauliflower tumbled in a dry masala of warming spices — a no-gravy North Indian staple that pairs perfectly with roti.
tip: Keep the lid on and resist adding water — the cauliflower releases enough moisture to cook everything through without making it watery.
method: Parboil potato cubes 5 min; drain.
Heat oil; splutter cumin. Add onion; cook until golden.
Add ginger, chili, and tomato; cook until soft and oil separates.
Stir in turmeric, coriander powder, and red chili; fry 1 min.
Add potatoes and cauliflower; stir to coat. Season with salt.
Cover and cook on low-medium 15 min, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are tender.
Sprinkle garam masala and coriander; toss and serve.

name: Bhindi Masala
blurb: Okra tossed with spiced onion-tomato masala until perfectly non-slimy and moreish — a North Indian favourite that converts even okra sceptics.
tip: High heat and a dry pan are the secret to slime-free bhindi — wash okra the night before and air-dry uncovered overnight.
ingredients: 300 g okra (bhindi, washed, dried completely, sliced)
method: Ensure okra is completely dry before cutting — moisture causes sliminess.
Heat oil on high; fry okra in a single layer until exterior is dry and lightly browned, 8–10 min. Remove.
In the same pan, fry cumin then onion until golden.
Add tomato and spices; cook until oil separates.
Return okra; toss gently to coat. Cook 3–4 min.
Finish with amchur and coriander; serve dry.

name: Paneer Bhurji
blurb: Scrambled spiced paneer with onion and tomato — the North Indian answer to scrambled eggs, ready in minutes and endlessly versatile.
tip: Do not overcook once the paneer is added — bhurji should be moist and crumbly, not dry or rubbery.
method: Heat oil; splutter cumin. Add onion; sauté until golden.
Add ginger-garlic paste and chili; fry 1 min.
Add tomato and spices; cook until masala thickens and oil separates.
Add crumbled paneer; stir and toss to coat. Cook 2–3 min.
Squeeze lemon; garnish with coriander. Serve with roti or pav.

name: Vegetable Pulao
blurb: Basmati rice cooked with whole spices and seasonal vegetables — lighter than biryani, quicker to make, and fragrant enough to stand alone.
tip: Do not stir after adding water — hands-off cooking preserves grain integrity and keeps each rice grain separate.
ingredients: fried onions and fresh mint to garnish
method: Heat ghee; add whole spices and let sizzle 30 sec.
Add onion; sauté until light golden.
Add ginger-garlic paste; cook 1 min.
Add vegetables and turmeric; stir 2 min.
Add drained rice; stir gently to coat with ghee.
Pour in water and salt; bring to a boil.
Reduce to very low heat, cover tightly, and cook 15 min. Rest 5 min before opening.
Fluff gently; garnish with fried onion and fresh mint.

name: Paneer Tikka Masala
blurb: Smoky grilled paneer cubes returned to a rich spiced tomato-cashew gravy — the tandoor flavour you do not need a clay oven to recreate.
tip: The char on the paneer is non-negotiable — it is what separates tikka masala from a plain paneer curry. Use a very hot pan and let the paneer sit undisturbed.
method: Mix yogurt, spices, ginger-garlic paste, and oil; marinate paneer at least 30 min.
Grill or pan-fry marinated paneer on high heat until charred on edges. Set aside.
Sauté onion puree until golden; add ginger-garlic paste.
Add tomato puree and spices; simmer until oil separates, about 10 min.
Stir in cashew paste and cream; simmer 3 min until thick.
Add grilled paneer; simmer 2 min. Crush and stir in kasuri methi. Serve with naan or rice.

name: Khichdi
blurb: Rice and moong dal simmered to a gentle porridge-like softness with ghee and cumin — India's ultimate comfort food, and the dish every grandmother swears by.
tip: The consistency is a personal choice — add another half-cup of water for a thinner flowing khichdi, or less for a stiffer version. Both are correct.
ingredients: ¼ cup yellow moong dal (split, skinless)
method: Wash rice and dal together; soak 10 min.
Heat ghee; add cumin and let splutter.
Add green chili and turmeric; fry 15 sec.
Add rice, dal, salt, and water; stir once.
Pressure cook 2–3 whistles, or simmer covered 20–25 min, until soft and porridge-like.
Add more ghee if desired; serve with papad and pickle.

name: Chapati (Roti)
blurb: Soft whole-wheat flatbread — the daily bread of India. Made fresh at every meal across the country, from Kashmir to Kanyakumari.
tip: A well-rested dough (20 min) and a hot tawa are the two things that make chapati soft. Press gently with a folded cloth as it puffs.
method: Mix flour and salt; add water gradually, kneading 5–8 min until smooth and elastic. Rest 15 min.
Divide into balls; roll each into a thin 6–7 inch circle, dusting with flour.
Cook on a hot tawa 30–40 sec until small bubbles appear; flip.
Cook 30 sec more; then hold directly over an open flame 10–15 sec until it puffs.
Brush with ghee; serve immediately.

name: Onion Pakora
blurb: Crispy, lacy fritters of thinly sliced onion bound in spiced gram flour batter — the ultimate Indian monsoon snack with a cup of chai.
tip: 170 °C — not screaming hot — ensures the inside cooks through before the outside burns.
method: Mix gram flour with chili, cumin, red chili powder, turmeric, coriander, and salt.
Add onion slices and toss; the onion releases moisture — add only 1–2 tbsp water if needed.
Heat oil to 170 °C; drop small clusters into oil.
Fry on medium-high 4–5 min, turning once, until golden and crisp.
Drain; sprinkle chaat masala. Serve immediately with mint chutney.

name: Pav Bhaji
blurb: A vibrant, well-seasoned mash of mixed vegetables cooked with butter and pav bhaji masala, served with toasted buttered buns — Mumbai street food at its best.
tip: Mash the bhaji directly in the pan while it cooks — the repetitive mashing creates the characteristic almost creamy texture.
ingredients: lemon wedges, raw onion and coriander to serve
method: Heat 2 tbsp butter; sauté onion until golden. Add capsicum; cook 2 min.
Add tomato and all spices; cook until oil separates, about 8 min.
Add mashed potato, cauliflower, and peas; mash everything together in the pan.
Add water to desired consistency; simmer 10 min, stirring often.
Adjust seasoning; top with remaining butter.
Slit pav buns; toast on a buttered tawa until golden. Serve with bhaji, lemon, onion, and coriander.

name: Kachori
blurb: Flaky, deep-fried pastry shells filled with spiced moong dal — a North Indian snack beloved from Rajasthan to Bengal.
tip: Fry kachoris low and slow — high heat browns the outside before the inside is cooked, leaving raw-tasting dough at the centre.
ingredients: ½ cup yellow moong dal (soaked, drained)
method: Mix flour, oil, and salt; add water gradually to make a firm dough. Rest 20 min.
Blend soaked dal coarsely. Fry with oil and all spices until dry and aromatic. Cool.
Divide dough; roll each into a small disc. Place filling, gather edges, and seal.
Flatten gently into a puri shape without tearing.
Deep fry on low-medium heat 8–10 min, turning frequently, until golden and crisp all through.
Serve hot with tamarind chutney and mint chutney.

name: Murukku
blurb: Crunchy, spiral-shaped rice flour snacks seasoned with cumin and sesame — a South Indian festival staple that disappears from the tin before you can blink.
tip: The dough must be firm enough to hold shape through the press — too soft and spirals collapse; too stiff and the dough cracks.
method: Mix both flours, spices, and butter; add hot water gradually to make a stiff but pliable dough.
Rest 5 min. Fill a murukku press or piping bag with a star nozzle.
Pipe spirals onto a greased surface or directly into oil.
Deep fry in batches at 160–170 °C, turning gently, until the sizzling subsides and murukku is crisp.
Drain; cool completely — they crisp up further as they cool.
Store airtight for up to 2 weeks.

name: Kheer (Rice Pudding)
blurb: Slow-cooked rice melted into creamy cardamom-scented full-fat milk, crowned with pistachios and rose petals — the quintessential Indian celebration dessert.
tip: Stir frequently and use a heavy pot — milk scorches easily on the base and leaves a burnt flavour throughout.
ingredients: pinch of saffron dissolved in 1 tbsp warm milk
method: Bring milk to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pot; add rice.
Simmer on low, stirring every 5 min, for 30–35 min until rice is very soft and milk reduced by one-third.
Add sugar and cardamom; stir until dissolved. Simmer 5 min more.
Stir in saffron milk and rose water; remove from heat.
Serve warm, or chill 2–3 hours. Garnish with nuts and rose petals before serving.

name: Gulab Jamun
blurb: Soft, doughnut-like milk solid balls soaked in saffron and cardamom-scented sugar syrup — served warm, they dissolve with almost startling ease.
tip: Fry on the lowest possible heat — gulab jamun must cook from inside out; high heat gives a dark shell with a raw doughy centre.
ingredients: 1 cup khoya (mawa, or use full-fat milk powder)
oil or ghee for deep frying
method: Boil sugar and water to a sticky syrup; add cardamom, saffron, and rose water. Keep warm.
Mix khoya, flour, and baking soda; add just enough milk and ghee to make a soft non-sticky dough.
Shape into smooth oval balls with no cracks.
Deep fry on very low heat, turning continuously, until dark golden brown, 8–10 min.
Drain briefly; soak immediately in warm syrup at least 30 min before serving.
Serve warm, 2–3 per portion.

name: Jalebi
blurb: Pretzel-shaped deep-fried batter spirals, crackling crisp and soaked to the core in warm saffron syrup — the joyous orange swirls of every Indian celebration.
tip: Syrup must be warm, not cold or boiling — cold syrup makes jalebi soggy, boiling syrup causes crystallisation on the surface.
method: Mix flour, yogurt, turmeric, and water into a smooth lump-free batter slightly thinner than dosa batter. Cover and ferment overnight.
Boil sugar and water to one-string consistency; add saffron, rose water, and cardamom. Keep warm.
Heat oil in a flat shallow pan to 170 °C. Fill a squeeze bottle with batter.
Pipe concentric circles into the oil; fry 2–3 min per side until crisp.
Drain briefly; soak in warm syrup 1–2 min. Serve immediately — jalebi are best eaten hot.

name: Besan Ladoo
blurb: Golden roasted gram flour balls bound with ghee and scented with cardamom — the celebratory sweet that every Indian household makes for festivals and happy occasions.
tip: Roast gram flour all the way to a deep golden colour — under-roasted besan leaves an unpleasant raw aftertaste in the finished ladoo.
method: Heat ghee in a heavy pan; add gram flour.
Roast on low heat, stirring continuously, 12–15 min until flour turns golden and smells nutty.
Remove from heat; cool until just warm.
Add icing sugar, cardamom, cashews, and raisins; mix well.
Shape into round balls while still warm — the mixture firms as it cools.
Cool completely; store airtight up to 2 weeks.

name: Masala Chai
blurb: Strong black tea simmered with ginger, cardamom, and spices in equal parts milk and water — India's unofficial national drink, comforting at any hour.
tip: Add the tea after the spices have had 2 minutes in the water — the spices open up first and infuse more deeply into the chai.
method: Bring water to a boil; add ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves.
Simmer 2 min to release the spices.
Add tea leaves; simmer 1 min.
Pour in milk; bring back to a gentle boil, then simmer 3–4 min until colour deepens.
Add sugar; stir to dissolve.
Strain into cups; serve hot.

name: Rava Kesari
blurb: Saffron-gold semolina halwa shimmering with ghee and studded with cashews — South India's festival sweet that doubles as a celebratory breakfast offering.
tip: Pour the boiling water all at once and stir fast — lumps form when water is added gradually. A smooth kesari has a silky, jewel-like finish.
method: Heat 1 tbsp ghee; fry cashews until golden; remove. Fry raisins until plump; remove.
Roast semolina in the same pan on medium, stirring, 4–5 min until fragrant.
Dissolve saffron in 2 tbsp warm water; add to the measured water.
Bring saffron water to a boil; pour carefully over roasted semolina.
Stir continuously on medium until water is absorbed and rava thickens.
Add sugar; stir vigorously — it loosens first, then thickens again.
Add remaining ghee in 2 additions, stirring between each, until glossy.
Fold in cashews, raisins, and cardamom. Serve warm.

name: Filter Coffee
blurb: Strong decoction drip-brewed through a brass filter, then mixed with hot frothy milk — the ritual morning cup of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
method: Add coffee powder to the upper compartment of a metal filter. Pour hot (not boiling) water over it and let the decoction drip through — takes 5–10 min.
Pour decoction and sugar into a tumbler.
Heat milk until steaming. Pour over the decoction.
Pour the mixture back and forth between the tumbler and davara several times to froth and aerate. Serve immediately.

name: Haldi Doodh (Golden Milk)
blurb: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, black pepper, and honey — an ancient Indian remedy that has become a global wellness staple.
method: Heat milk in a saucepan over medium heat.
Add turmeric, black pepper, cardamom and ginger. Stir well.
Simmer 5 minutes without boiling.
Remove from heat. Stir in honey.
Strain into a mug and serve hot.

name: Badam Milk (Almond Milk)
blurb: Saffron-tinted warm milk enriched with ground soaked almonds and cardamom — festive, nourishing, and loved from Kashmir to Kerala.
method: Dissolve saffron in 1 tbsp warm milk and set aside.
Blend soaked almonds with 1/4 cup milk to a very smooth paste.
Heat remaining milk. Add sugar, cardamom and saffron milk. Stir to combine.
Stir in almond paste. Simmer on low 5–7 minutes, stirring continuously.
Pour into a glass and garnish with sliced pistachios. Serve hot or chilled.

name: Ginger Lemon Tea
blurb: A sharp, cleansing brew of fresh ginger and black tea brightened with lemon and honey — a brisk, energising start to the morning.
method: Bring water to a boil with ginger slices. Reduce heat, simmer 3 minutes.
Add tea leaves and steep 2 minutes.
Strain into a cup.
Stir in lemon juice and honey. Serve hot.

name: Nimbu Pani (Indian Lemonade)
blurb: Fresh lime juice in chilled water with a pinch of black salt and roasted cumin — India's ubiquitous street cooler, endlessly refreshing in any season.
method: Combine lime juice, sugar, black salt and cumin powder in a tall glass.
Add chilled water and stir until sugar dissolves.
Add ice cubes and fresh mint sprigs.
Taste and adjust salt or sugar. Serve immediately.

name: Chaas / Mor (Spiced Buttermilk)
blurb: Thin, savory yogurt whisked with water, curry leaves and ginger — a cooling digestive served at the end of a South Indian or Gujarati meal.
method: Whisk yogurt until completely smooth with no lumps.
Add cold water gradually, whisking to a thin, even consistency.
Stir in green chilli, ginger, cumin powder and salt.
Pour into glasses, garnish with curry leaves and coriander. Serve chilled.

name: Aam Panna (Raw Mango Cooler)
blurb: A tangy-sweet raw mango concentrate with roasted cumin and black salt — the definitive Indian summer cooler, great for heat and digestion.
method: Boil or pressure-cook the whole mango until completely soft, about 10–15 min.
Cool, peel and squeeze out all the pulp. Discard skin and seed.
Blend pulp with sugar, cumin, black salt, a pinch of salt and mint until smooth.
Refrigerate the concentrate. To serve: stir 3 tbsp concentrate into a glass of cold water. Add ice and mint.

name: Jal Jeera
blurb: A zesty spiced water drink made with cumin, fresh mint, tamarind and black salt — a traditional digestive served before meals at Indian street stalls.
ingredients: Tamarind — a small ball (soaked in 1/4 cup water)
method: Blend mint, ginger and green chilli with 2 tbsp water to a smooth paste.
Squeeze soaked tamarind through the water to extract pulp; discard fibre.
Combine mint paste, tamarind water, cumin, black salt, lemon juice and sugar in a pitcher.
Add cold water, stir and strain into glasses over ice. Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Kokum Sharbat
blurb: A deep-purple cooler from the Konkan coast — sun-dried kokum steeped into a tart, sweet syrup then diluted with chilled water.
method: Soak kokum in 1/2 cup warm water for 15–20 minutes until softened.
Squeeze and press to extract juice. Discard solids.
Add sugar and heat briefly to dissolve. Cool completely.
To serve: add 2–3 tbsp concentrate to a glass of cold water. Stir in cumin and rock salt. Add ice.

name: Rose Milk
blurb: Cold milk sweetened with fragrant rose syrup — a street-stall classic from Tamil Nadu, simple, pink, and deeply nostalgic.
method: If using basil seeds, soak in 2 tbsp water for 10 minutes until they bloom translucent.
Pour cold milk into a tall glass.
Add rose syrup and stir until milk turns evenly pink.
Add ice cubes and soaked basil seeds if using. Serve immediately.

name: Warm Ginger Honey Tea
blurb: A soothing caffeine-free brew of fresh ginger and tulsi with honey and lemon — ideal after dinner to aid digestion and ease into rest.
method: Bring water to a boil with ginger and tulsi leaves.
Reduce heat and simmer 5–7 minutes.
Strain into a mug.
Stir in honey and a squeeze of lemon. Sip warm.

name: Tomato Chutney
blurb: A tangy-spicy tomato relish cooked with onion, garlic and tamarind — robust enough to stand up to a crisp dosa or plain idli.
method: Heat oil in a pan. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add asafoetida and curry leaves.
Add onion, garlic and dried red chillies. Saute until onion is golden, about 5 minutes.
Add chopped tomatoes, tamarind and salt. Cook on medium heat until tomatoes are completely mushy and oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Cool slightly. Blend to a coarse chutney. Serve at room temperature.

name: Mint-Coriander Chutney
blurb: A vivid green chutney of fresh mint and coriander with lemon and green chilli — the universal Indian dip that lifts every snack and meal.
method: Add all ingredients to a blender: coriander, mint, green chillies, garlic, ginger, lemon juice, cumin, salt and water.
Blend until smooth, scraping down the sides as needed. Add a little more water if required.
Taste and adjust salt and lemon juice.
Transfer to an airtight container and refrigerate until needed. Best used the same day.

name: Sambar
blurb: A South Indian lentil soup fragrant with tamarind, vegetables and sambar powder — the irreplaceable accompaniment to idli, dosa, and steamed rice.
ingredients: Tamarind — lemon-sized ball (soaked in 1 cup warm water)
method: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric and 1.5 cups water until completely soft (2–3 whistles). Mash well.
Extract tamarind juice by squeezing the soaked ball through the water; discard fibre.
In a pot, bring tamarind water to boil. Add shallots, tomatoes, drumstick and salt. Cook 10 minutes until vegetables are tender.
Add sambar powder and the mashed dal. Stir and simmer 10 more minutes. Adjust consistency with water.
In a small pan heat oil. Add mustard seeds — let splutter. Add dried red chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida. Pour tempering over sambar. Serve hot.

name: Groundnut Chutney (Peanut Chutney)
blurb: Roasted peanuts ground with garlic and chilli into a rich, nutty chutney — hearty, protein-rich and a bold alternative to coconut chutney.
method: In a dry pan, lightly roast peanuts until fragrant if not already roasted. Cool.
Grind peanuts, garlic, red chillies, tamarind and salt with just enough water to a slightly coarse chutney — not too smooth.
Transfer to a bowl.
Heat oil, add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add curry leaves and asafoetida. Pour tempering over chutney.
Mix and serve with idli, dosa or vada.

name: Nannari Sarbath
blurb: Refreshing Indian sarsaparilla syrup drink served chilled — cooling and aromatic.
method: Mix nannari syrup with chilled water
Add lemon juice and stir
Serve over ice

name: Panakam
blurb: Traditional South Indian jaggery drink spiced with cardamom and dry ginger.
method: Dissolve jaggery in water
Add spices and lemon juice
Stir well and serve

name: Ragi Kanji (Finger Millet Porridge)
blurb: Nourishing finger millet porridge — a South Indian breakfast drink rich in iron and calcium.
method: Mix ragi flour with a little water into a smooth paste
Boil remaining water; whisk in ragi paste
Cook on low heat 5 min stirring constantly
Add salt; serve warm

name: Idli Podi (Gun Powder Chutney)
blurb: Spicy dry chutney powder of roasted lentils and chillies, served with sesame oil alongside idli and dosa.
method: Dry roast dals and chillies separately until golden
Cool completely
Grind coarsely with salt and asafoetida
Mix in sesame seeds
Serve with sesame oil

name: Lemon Rice (Chitranna)
blurb: Tangy South Indian rice tempered with mustard seeds, peanuts, and lemon juice — a beloved one-pot meal.
method: Heat oil; splutter mustard seeds
Add peanuts, curry leaves, chillies; fry 1 min
Add turmeric and cooked rice
Mix in lemon juice and salt
Toss well and serve

name: Bisi Bele Bath
blurb: Karnataka's iconic one-pot comfort dish of rice, toor dal, vegetables, and warming spices.
method: Pressure cook rice, dal, and vegetables together
Add tamarind paste and masala powder; simmer until thick
Prepare tempering with mustard seeds and cashews in ghee
Pour tempering over bath; serve hot

name: Vangi Bath (Brinjal Rice)
blurb: Karnataka-style spiced brinjal rice with a fragrant masala — hearty, tangy, and flavourful.
method: Sauté brinjal in oil until tender
Add masala powder and tamarind paste; cook 2 min
Mix in cooked rice and salt
Toss with curry leaves and serve

name: Olan (Ash Gourd Coconut Curry)
blurb: Light Kerala curry of ash gourd and black-eyed peas simmered in coconut milk — a quintessential Onam Sadya dish.
method: Cook ash gourd with green chillies and salt until tender
Add black-eyed peas and coconut milk
Simmer on low heat 5 min
Finish with coconut oil and curry leaves

name: Thoran (Vegetable Stir-fry with Coconut)
blurb: Kerala-style dry vegetable stir-fry with freshly grated coconut — simple, nutritious, and aromatic.
method: Heat oil; splutter mustard seeds, chillies, curry leaves
Add vegetables with turmeric and salt
Cover and cook on low heat 8 min
Mix in grated coconut; cook 2 more min and serve

name: Mango Achar (Pickle)
blurb: Pungent and spicy mango pickle — an indispensable condiment alongside parathas and dal.
method: Mix spices with mustard oil
Toss mango pieces in spiced oil
Store in airtight jar
Serve as condiment

name: Dahi (Fresh Curd)
blurb: Plain set curd — the simplest and most essential accompaniment in Indian cooking. Eaten with rice, roti, or on its own at every meal.
tip: Set curd at home by adding a teaspoon of live curd to warm (not hot) milk and leaving it undisturbed for 6–8 hours.
method: Boil milk and cool to lukewarm
Add starter culture and mix gently
Cover and leave undisturbed 6–8 hours
Refrigerate once set

name: Makhan (White Butter)
blurb: Fresh homemade white butter — the classic Punjabi accompaniment to hot parathas.
method: Churn fresh cream in a blender with cold water
Strain off the butter as it separates
Wash with cold water
Serve immediately

name: Hari Chutney (Mint-Coriander Chutney)
blurb: Vibrant green chutney made with fresh mint and coriander — the essential dipping sauce for North Indian snacks.
method: Blend all ingredients to a smooth paste
Adjust salt and lemon juice
Serve fresh; refrigerates up to 3 days

name: Boondi Raita
blurb: Crispy boondi pearls soaked in spiced yogurt — refreshing and cooling.
method: Soak boondi in warm water 10 min; drain
Whisk curd smooth and add spices
Mix in boondi
Garnish with coriander and chill before serving

name: Sattu Sharbat
blurb: Rustic high-protein drink from Bihar and UP made with roasted gram flour, jaggery, and spices.
method: Mix sattu in a glass of water until lump-free
Add jaggery, lemon juice, cumin, and black salt
Stir well
Serve chilled

name: Thandai
blurb: Festive North Indian spiced milk drink with almonds, rose petals, and fennel — served chilled.
method: Grind almonds, seeds, and spices to a paste
Blend with milk, sugar, and rose water
Strain through a fine sieve
Chill and serve garnished with saffron

name: Shikanji (Spiced Lemonade)
blurb: Classic North Indian lemonade with black salt, cumin, and mint — cooling, tangy, and refreshing.
method: Mix lemon juice, sugar, and spices in water
Stir until sugar dissolves
Serve over ice with fresh mint

name: Chana Masala
blurb: Robust North Indian chickpea curry with tomatoes, onion, and warming whole spices.
method: Sauté onion in oil until golden
Add ginger-garlic paste and tomatoes; cook until oil separates
Add chana masala powder and chickpeas
Simmer 10 min
Garnish with coriander and serve

name: Tandoori Roti
blurb: Whole-wheat flatbread baked in a tandoor or heavy skillet — soft inside with slightly charred edges.
method: Mix flour, yogurt, salt, and water into a soft dough; rest 30 min
Roll into thick circles
Cook on a very hot cast-iron pan or in oven at 230°C
Finish on flame until charred spots appear
Brush with butter

name: Puri
blurb: Deep-fried unleavened whole wheat bread — light, puffed, and beloved at festive North Indian meals.
method: Mix flour, oil, and salt; knead with water into a firm dough
Roll into small thin discs
Deep fry in hot oil until puffed and golden
Drain and serve immediately

name: Bhatura
blurb: Fluffy, deep-fried leavened bread — the iconic companion to Chole in the beloved Chole Bhatura combination.
method: Mix flour, yogurt, baking soda, sugar, and salt into a soft dough
Rest 2 hours covered
Roll into oval shapes
Deep fry in hot oil until puffed and golden
Serve immediately with chole

name: Tender Coconut Water
blurb: Fresh, naturally sweet coconut water — nature's electrolyte drink, hydrating and cooling.
method: Open fresh tender coconut
Pour chilled water into glass
Serve immediately

name: Fruit salad 1
blurb: Community recipe.
tip: Essentially a power-packed breakfast or snack bowl
tags: High in natural sugars for quick energy
but balanced with protein and micronutrients
ingredients: Pinch of garden cress (halim or alive)
method: Heat the Milk to a medrate temperature and put all the ingredients together. Allow the mixture to soak for 15 min and then serve.

name: Black Coffee
blurb: Black coffee made from Indian filter coffee powder (typically a blend of Arabica and chicory) is a ritual across South India. The gentle roast and chicory addition give South Indian coffee its characteristic deep colour and slightly sweet bitterness that sets it apart from international coffee styles.
tip: Do not pour boiling water; water that is too hot makes coffee bitter. Let the kettle rest 30 seconds after boiling.
method: Measure coffee powder into a cup.
Bring water to a boil (not a rolling boil — around 90°C is ideal).
Pour hot water over coffee.
Stir and serve black, or add a splash of milk if desired.

name: Thepla
blurb: Thepla is Gujarat's everyday flatbread and its ultimate travel companion — spiced with methi, eaten at breakfast, packed in dabbas and served on train journeys across India. A freshly made thepla with thick curd is a Gujarati morning in a single bite.
tip: The dough should be soft; if it springs back on rolling, rest it 5 more minutes before rolling again.
ingredients: Fresh fenugreek leaves — ½ cup, chopped
method: Knead whole wheat flour, besan, methi, ginger paste, turmeric, chilli powder, curd and oil into a soft dough.
Divide into balls; roll into thin circles.
Cook on a hot tawa with a drizzle of oil until golden spots appear on both sides.
Serve warm with curd, pickle or chundo.

name: Thalipeeth
blurb: Thalipeeth is Maharashtra's multi-grain flatbread — traditionally made with bhajni, a pre-roasted flour blend of jowar, bajra, wheat and besan. Nutritionally among the richest Indian flatbreads, it is the everyday breakfast of rural Maharashtra and a celebrated revival dish in urban health circles.
tip: Work quickly — the multi-grain dough dries out faster than wheat dough; keep a bowl of water nearby.
method: Mix all flours (jowar, bajra, besan, wheat) with onion, green chilli, coriander, turmeric and salt.
Add water gradually to form a soft, pliable dough.
Flatten a portion between wet palms into a round patty directly on a hot oiled griddle.
Cook covered on medium heat 4 minutes; flip and cook uncovered until done.
Serve hot with curd, chutney or thecha (green chilli relish).

name: Misal Pav
blurb: Misal Pav is Maharashtra's most regional dish — every city has its own version. Pune's is mild; Nashik's is aggressive; Kolhapur's is incendiary. The sprouted moth bean is the soul of the dish, making it a nutritionally dense street food that sustains market workers through a full morning.
tip: Sprout the matki at home (soak 8 hrs, tie in cloth, rest 24 hrs) for maximum nutrition and flavour.
method: Heat oil; add sprouted matki, onion and tomato; sauté 3 minutes.
Add misal masala and ½ cup water; cover and cook 10 minutes until sprouts are soft.
Season with salt. The rassa (gravy) should be thin and spicy.
Toast and lightly butter the pav.
Serve the misal in a bowl topped with onion, coriander, farsan and a squeeze of lemon; pav on the side.

name: Neer Dosa
blurb: Neer Dosa (water dosa) is Coastal Karnataka's most ethereal creation — a diaphanous, snow-white, lace-edged crepe made from nothing but rice and water. Its delicacy is the point; it is the antithesis of the thick, crispy dosa. Konkani households serve it at breakfast and dinner with fish curry or coconut chutney.
tip: Pour from height to create a naturally thin, holey crepe — ladling and spreading makes it too thick.
method: Soak raw rice 4 hours; grind with water to an extremely thin, watery batter.
Add salt; the batter should pour like water.
Heat a non-stick or cast-iron griddle; grease lightly with oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter from a height — do not spread; let it flow naturally into a thin circle.
Cover and cook 2 minutes until the dosa is set and the edges lift. Do not flip.
Fold gently and serve immediately with coconut chutney.

name: Akki Rotti
blurb: Akki Rotti is Karnataka's rice flour flatbread — a naturally gluten-free, protein-rich breakfast that North Karnataka households have eaten for generations. Unlike chapati rolled on a board, akki rotti is patted directly onto the hot tawa with a wet hand — a technique that takes practice.
tip: Wet your palm generously before patting; a dry hand makes the rotti tear.
method: Mix rice flour with onion, green chilli, coriander, sesame, coconut and salt; add water to make a soft pliable dough.
Divide into balls. Wet your palm and flatten each ball directly on a hot oiled griddle.
Cook covered on medium heat 3–4 minutes; flip and cook uncovered until golden.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or saagu.

name: Bajra Roti with Ghee and Jaggery
blurb: Bajra Roti with Ghee and Jaggery is Rajasthan's oldest breakfast — pearl millet flatbread that sustained desert communities through harsh winters and scarce resources. Bajra is uniquely warming among all millets, making it the ideal grain for Rajasthan's cold desert mornings.
tip: Bajra dough dries out instantly; roll and cook each roti one at a time, never preparing in advance.
method: Knead bajra flour with salt and enough warm water to form a stiff dough (bajra does not bind like wheat).
Divide into balls; pat each into a thick round between palms — it will crack; patch as you go.
Cook on a hot dry tawa until charred spots appear on both sides and the roti feels firm.
Serve immediately with ghee and a small piece of jaggery on the side.

name: Missi Roti
blurb: Missi Roti is Rajasthan's spiced flatbread — a protein-rich combination of whole wheat and besan that is the everyday breakfast of rural Rajasthan and increasingly celebrated in health-focused kitchens. Methi leaves add a slightly bitter edge that contrasts beautifully with rich dals.
tip: The dough softens as the besan hydrates — let it rest 10 minutes before rolling for easier handling.
ingredients: Fresh fenugreek leaves — ¼ cup, chopped
method: Mix all flours (wheat, besan, methi leaves), onion, green chilli, ajwain, chilli powder, turmeric and salt.
Add water and oil gradually to form a soft, pliable dough.
Divide into balls; roll into medium-thick rounds.
Cook on a hot tawa with a drizzle of oil until golden on both sides.
Serve hot with curd, pickle and green chutney.

name: Jolpan
blurb: Jolpan is Assam's traditional morning offering — poha, curd, jaggery and fresh coconut served during Bihu festivals. A no-cook dish that celebrates the valley's abundance of rice and fresh produce.
tip: Use thick curd and ripe banana for natural sweetness; adjust jaggery to taste.
method: Soak poha in water 2 minutes; drain well and squeeze out excess liquid.
Mix curd, jaggery and a pinch of salt until smooth.
Add drained poha, sesame seeds, grated coconut and banana.
Toss gently and serve at room temperature or slightly chilled.

name: Pakhala Bhata
blurb: Pakhala Bhata is Odisha's ancient summer staple — fermented water-soaked rice eaten cold with raw vegetables and mustard oil. In the scorching Odia summers, pakhala cools the body from within. It is not just food but cultural identity — every year Pakhala Dibasa (Pakhala Day) is celebrated.
tip: The overnight fermentation is what makes it pakhala — same-day soaking is just watered rice.
method: Soak cooked rice in 2 cups of water for 8 hours or overnight (pakhala ferments slightly).
In the morning, add curd and a pinch of salt; stir.
Prepare accompaniments: slice cucumber and onion, slit green chillies.
Serve the pakhala in a bowl topped with cucumber, onion, green chilli and a drizzle of mustard oil.
Eat by mixing everything together.

name: Muri with Coconut and Banana
blurb: Muri with Coconut and Banana is a classic Bengali bhaater hotel breakfast — simple, nourishing and deeply comforting. Puffed rice softened in water is an ancient way to make rice digestible first thing in the morning, and the combination with coconut and jaggery provides balanced energy.
tip: Soak muri for exactly 1 minute — longer and it turns to paste; shorter and it stays hard.
method: Soak puffed rice in water for 1 minute; drain and squeeze gently — it should be soft but not soggy.
In a bowl, combine the softened muri with grated coconut, sliced banana and jaggery.
Add a pinch of salt and a few drops of mustard oil; mix gently.
Serve immediately as a morning snack.

name: Radhaballabhi
blurb: Radhaballabhi is a treasured Bengali breakfast puri — a maida puri stuffed with spiced urad dal filling, named after the deity Radha and Ballabh (another name for Krishna). Served at Durga Puja and special morning meals, it is always paired with cholar dal.
tip: Fry on medium heat, not high; a very hot oil seals the surface before the inside cooks through.
method: Drain soaked urad dal; grind coarsely with fennel, ginger, green chilli and salt to a thick filling.
Make a stiff dough with maida and a little oil and water.
Roll small rounds, place filling in the centre, seal and flatten into thick discs.
Deep-fry in medium-hot oil, turning frequently, until puffed and golden.
Serve hot with cholar dal or aloo dum.

name: Puttu with Kadala Curry
blurb: Puttu with Kadala Curry is Kerala's defining breakfast combination — steamed rice and coconut cylinders paired with a dark, robust black chickpea curry. The puttu's neutral starchiness and the kadala's earthy depth create a balance that Kerala mornings are built around.
tip: The rice flour texture for puttu must feel like wet sand when squeezed — too wet and it steams into a solid block.
method: Steam puttu: mix rice flour with water (crumbly texture), layer with coconut in a puttu maker and steam 8 minutes.
Soak black chickpeas overnight; pressure cook until very tender.
Heat oil; sauté onion until golden. Add tomato, turmeric and garam masala; cook 5 min.
Add coconut milk and cooked kadala; simmer 15 minutes until thick.
Serve puttu broken over the kadala curry — they are meant to be mixed.

name: Idiyappam with Coconut Milk
blurb: Idiyappam with Coconut Milk is Kerala's most delicate breakfast — steamed string hoppers made fresh each morning, eaten with sweetened coconut milk drawn from freshly grated coconut. In Malabar households it is a Sunday ritual; in Travancore, an everyday comfort.
tip: The batter must be smooth and flowing — too thick and the strings break; too thin and they merge together.
method: Mix rice flour with a pinch of salt and water to form a smooth, thin batter.
Press batter through an idiyappam press or chakli maker into circular nest shapes on steamer plates.
Steam 8–10 minutes until cooked through.
Warm coconut milk with jaggery and cardamom until jaggery dissolves; do not boil.
Serve idiyappam with the warm sweetened coconut milk poured over.

name: Mooli Paratha
blurb: Mooli Paratha is Punjab's winter breakfast staple — a whole wheat flatbread stuffed with fresh white radish that is grated, squeezed and spiced. Eaten through the cold months when mooli is at its sweetest, it is one of the great comfort breakfasts of North India.
tip: Squeezing out all the mooli water is critical — wet filling makes the paratha soggy and difficult to roll.
method: Grate mooli; add salt and rest 5 minutes. Squeeze out all the water firmly.
Mix squeezed mooli with green chilli, ginger, ajwain and cumin powder.
Make a dough with wheat flour, salt and water; rest 15 min.
Stuff mooli filling into dough balls; roll into parathas.
Cook with oil on a hot tawa until golden on both sides.

name: Kozhukattai
blurb: Kozhukattai is Tamil Nadu's steamed dumpling — known as modak in Maharashtra and offered to Lord Ganesha during Vinayagar Chaturthi. The rice flour outer skin becomes gloriously translucent when steamed, revealing the coconut-jaggery filling within.
tip: Keep the dough warm and covered while shaping — cold dough cracks at the edges when you bring them together.
method: Mix rice flour with a pinch of salt and coconut; gradually add hot water to form a soft dough.
Add jaggery and cardamom to the grated coconut filling; mix well.
Take a small ball of dough; flatten in your palm; place filling in centre.
Bring edges together and shape into a smooth dumpling (modak shape).
Steam for 10 minutes until the outer skin turns translucent.
Serve warm with a drizzle of ghee.

name: Enduri Pitha
blurb: Enduri Pitha is Odisha's most aromatic pitha — steamed inside turmeric leaves, which impart a distinctive earthy-golden fragrance to the sweet coconut-jaggery filling. Made during Prathamashtami (the festival honouring the eldest child), it is one of Odisha's most culturally specific dishes.
tip: If turmeric leaves are unavailable, banana leaves work — but the characteristic turmeric flavour is lost.
method: Soak rice and urad dal separately; blend each separately then combine.
Mix in grated coconut, jaggery and cardamom to the batter.
