Wash turmeric leaves; place a spoonful of batter on each leaf and fold to enclose.
Arrange in a steamer; steam 15–18 minutes until the batter is set.
Unwrap and eat straight from the leaf — the turmeric imparts a subtle earthiness.

name: Makki di Roti
blurb: Makki di Roti is Punjab's winter icon — the thick, slightly grainy maize flatbread that is inseparable from sarson ka saag (mustard greens). Eaten from November through February when mustard fields bloom across the Punjab plains, it is a seasonal ritual as much as a meal.
tip: Maize dough cracks easily — keep a bowl of water nearby and patch cracks as you pat.
method: Knead makki atta with methi leaves, green chilli, ginger and salt using warm water — it will be stiffer than wheat dough.
Divide into balls; pat each ball between wet palms into a thick round (it cracks easily — this is normal; patch the cracks).
Cook on a dry tawa on medium heat until both sides have golden spots and the roti is cooked through.
Spread generously with ghee; serve hot with sarson ka saag, jaggery and raw onion.

name: Dal Baati Churma
blurb: Dal Baati Churma is Rajasthan's ceremonial meal — hard wheat dumplings (baati) baked in desert sand or a wood fire, served with five-lentil dal and sweet churma. Originally the food of Rajput warriors who could bake baati in embers while on the move, it is now Rajasthan's proudest culinary symbol.
tip: Generous ghee is not optional; it is the dish. Dal Baati Churma eaten without ghee is not Dal Baati Churma.
method: Make baati: mix wheat flour, semolina, ghee and salt; add water to form a stiff dough. Shape into round balls. Bake at 200°C for 30 minutes until golden, or roast in an oven directly on the rack.
Make panchmel dal: pressure cook all dals together with turmeric. Temper with ghee, red chilli, cumin seeds and hing.
Make churma: crush two baatis coarsely; add jaggery, ghee and cardamom; mix.
Crack baatis open, pour ghee over each. Serve baati, dal and churma together.

name: Gatte ki Sabzi
blurb: Gatte ki Sabzi is Rajasthan's most ingenious dish — besan cylinders boiled until firm and then simmered in a spiced curd gravy. In a desert state where fresh vegetables were historically scarce, gatte was a protein-rich alternative that kept for days.
tip: Boil gatte in plenty of water; they swell slightly and need room. Crowded gatte stick together.
method: Mix besan, coriander powder, turmeric, chilli powder, ajwain, fennel and oil into a stiff dough using a little water.
Roll into a thick log; cut into cylinders (gatte).
Boil gatte in salted water 8–10 minutes until firm; remove and slice.
Whisk curd with besan, red chilli and remaining spices; cook in a pan stirring constantly until it thickens to a curry.
Add sliced gatte; simmer 5 minutes. Finish with a mustard tempering.

name: Ker Sangri
blurb: Ker Sangri is Rajasthan's desert pickle-vegetable — two wild desert plants (ker berry and sangri bean) that were foraged and sun-dried for preservation across the Thar Desert. The dried vegetables require soaking and the dish has an intense, concentrated flavour found nowhere else in Indian cuisine.
tip: Soak ker and sangri for at least 8 hours; under-soaked ker retains a bitter astringency.
method: Drain soaked ker and sangri; pat dry.
Heat oil; add whole red chilli and let it bloom.
Add ker and sangri; fry on medium heat 3 minutes.
Add curd, red chilli powder, coriander powder, turmeric and amchur; cook until oil surfaces and the masala clings to the vegetables.
Adjust salt; serve with bajra roti.

name: Dal Dhokli
blurb: Dal Dhokli is Gujarat's one-pot comfort meal — wheat strips simmered in tangy-sweet toor dal until they absorb its character. The simultaneous sweetness of jaggery, sourness of tamarind and warmth of spices reflects the Gujarati palate's love of balanced flavour.
tip: Add dhokli strips one by one so they do not clump; stir gently every 5 minutes.
method: Boil toor dal with turmeric until completely soft; keep aside.
Make wheat dough with salt and a little oil; rest 15 min. Roll into strips.
In the cooked dal, add tamarind, jaggery, red chilli powder, coriander powder and mustard tempering.
Drop dough strips into simmering dal and cook 15 minutes until dhokli is cooked through.
Finish with ghee and coriander. The dish thickens as it sits.

name: Undhiyu
blurb: Undhiyu is Gujarat's winter festival dish — a slow-cooked medley of seasonal vegetables and steamed fenugreek dumplings named for the clay pot (undhu = upside down) it was traditionally cooked in underground. Entire Gujarati families gather to cook it for Uttarayan (Makar Sankranti).
tip: Do not lift the lid during cooking — the steam builds the dish's flavour; every lid-lift loses 5 minutes of progress.
method: Make muthia: mix besan, wheat flour, methi, ginger-chilli paste and salt; shape into small cylinders and steam 15 min.
Boil all the hard vegetables (yam, raw banana, sweet potato) partially.
Grind coconut, coriander, green chilli and a little oil into a coarse masala.
Layer vegetables and muthia in a heavy pan; spread masala between layers.
Pour oil over the top; cook covered on very low heat 25 minutes without stirring.
Toss gently once done and serve.

name: Aloo Posto
blurb: Aloo Posto is quintessential Bengali soul food — white poppy seeds (posto) ground into a paste that coats potato with a nutty, creamy richness. In Bengal, posto is not just an ingredient but an identity; no monsoon meal is complete without it.
tip: Grind posto with a little water to a fine paste — any coarseness makes the dish gritty.
method: Boil cubed potatoes until just tender; drain.
Heat mustard oil; add slit green chillies and let them sizzle.
Add boiled potatoes and turmeric; stir to coat.
Add poppy seed paste (grind 3 tbsp posto with 2 tbsp water); mix well.
Cook on low 5 minutes until oil separates. Season with salt.

name: Cholar Dal
blurb: Cholar Dal is Bengal's festive dal, served at pujas and weddings — the sweetness of grated coconut against the earthy chana dal, fragrant with whole spices and ghee, makes it unlike any other dal in the subcontinent. It is paired with deep-fried luchi (puri).
tip: Do not overcook chana dal; it should hold its shape. Mushy dal loses the dish's distinct texture.
method: Pressure cook chana dal until soft but not mushy (2 whistles).
Heat ghee; add bay leaf, cardamom, clove and cinnamon; let them bloom.
Add ginger; sauté briefly.
Add cooked dal, fresh coconut and salt; simmer 8 minutes.
Garnish with a final drizzle of ghee and serve with luchi or rice.

name: Shorshe Begun
blurb: Shorshe Begun is Bengal's mustardy masterpiece — whole brinjals stuffed with a sharp paste of ground mustard, poppy seeds and green chilli, then cooked in their own steam. The combination of mustard heat and poppy creaminess is a uniquely Bengali flavour profile.
tip: Use sharp, freshly ground mustard paste; store-bought paste is often stale and lacks the necessary bite.
method: Slit long brinjals carefully — keep stalks on; mix mustard paste, poppy paste, green chilli paste, turmeric and salt.
Stuff the paste gently into the slits of each brinjal.
Heat mustard oil to smoking; carefully place stuffed brinjals in.
Cover and cook on very low heat 12–15 minutes, turning once, until brinjals are tender.
Serve with steamed rice — the paste is the sauce.

name: Bharli Vangi
blurb: Bharli Vangi is Maharashtra's stuffed brinjal masterpiece — small purple brinjals packed with a nutty, coconut-peanut filling and cooked in their own steam. Goda masala, the sweet-spiced Maharashtrian blend, is what makes this dish unmistakably Marathi.
tip: Choose small, firm brinjals of equal size so they cook evenly and hold their shape.
ingredients: Peanuts — ¼ cup, roasted and ground
method: Mix peanuts, sesame seeds, dried coconut, coriander-cumin powder and goda masala into a dry filling.
Slit brinjals from the bottom, keeping the stem intact; stuff filling into each.
Heat oil in a wide pan; place stuffed brinjals carefully.
Add remaining filling and ½ cup water; cover and cook on low heat 20 minutes, turning once.
Uncover and cook 5 more minutes until oil surfaces and brinjals are fully soft.

name: Varan Bhaat
blurb: Varan Bhaat is Maharashtra's most primal comfort meal — the simplest preparation of toor dal poured over hot rice with ghee. It is the first solid food given to children, the food craved in illness, and the dish served at the end of the most elaborate wedding feasts.
tip: The varan should be watery, not thick; it pools into the rice rather than sitting on top.
method: Wash and pressure cook toor dal with turmeric until very soft (3 whistles).
Lightly mash the dal; add kokum petals and salt.
Heat ghee in a small pan; add mustard seeds — pour over the dal once they splutter.
Serve the varan over hot steamed rice with a drizzle of extra ghee on top.

name: Dalma
blurb: Dalma is Odisha's defining dal dish — a medley of toor dal cooked with seasonal vegetables and finished with coconut and panch phoron. It is a prasad (sacred offering) at Puri's Jagannath Temple and is served in the Mahaprasad — one of the world's largest community kitchens.
tip: Add vegetables in order of cooking time; drumstick needs 15 minutes, pumpkin only 8.
method: Boil toor dal with turmeric until soft; keep aside.
In a separate pot, cook all vegetables (raw banana, drumstick, pumpkin, brinjal) with a little water, panch phoron and turmeric.
Add cooked dal to the vegetables; mix gently.
Heat ghee; add dry red chillies and pour over the dalma.
Add fresh grated coconut; stir, adjust salt and serve with rice.

name: Potala Rasa
blurb: Potala Rasa is one of Odisha's most beloved vegetable curries — pointed gourd (parwal) cooked in a light, tomato-based gravy with the distinctive panch phoron tempering that marks all Odia and Bengali cooking. In Odisha, potol (pointed gourd) is revered enough to appear as a Jagannath Temple offering.
tip: Do not overcook pointed gourd; it becomes mushy quickly. It should hold its shape in the finished dish.
method: Slit pointed gourds along the length without cutting through; season inside with salt.
Heat oil; add panch phoron; let it splutter.
Add potatoes and fry 3 minutes.
Add tomato, ginger paste, turmeric, cumin and coriander powder; cook until oil surfaces.
Add pointed gourds and ½ cup water; cover and simmer 15 minutes until fully tender.
Adjust salt; serve with rice.

name: Sol Kadhi
blurb: Sol Kadhi is Konkan's digestive cooler — a pale pink, tangy-spiced drink made from kokum and coconut milk that doubles as a beverage and a digestive curry. Along coastal Maharashtra and Goa, it is drunk straight from a glass after a fish meal to soothe the stomach.
tip: Never heat Sol Kadhi — warmth separates the coconut milk and destroys the pink colour.
ingredients: Kokum (sol) — 10 petals, soaked in warm water
method: Extract kokum colour and flavour by soaking petals in ½ cup warm water for 15 minutes; squeeze and strain.
Add coconut milk to the kokum water.
Add finely chopped green chilli, grated ginger and salt; stir well.
Garnish with coriander. Serve cold or at room temperature — never heat Sol Kadhi.

name: Dum Aloo Kashmiri
blurb: Kashmiri Dum Aloo is defined by what it does not contain — no onion, no garlic, no tomato. The sauce is built entirely from whole spices and whisked curd, giving it a pale, ivory warmth that is deeply aromatic but not red-orange like its Punjabi counterpart. A signature of the Kashmiri Pandit kitchen.
tip: Fry the potatoes until the skin blisters; this prevents them absorbing too much gravy and going mushy.
method: Heat mustard oil to smoking; add baby potatoes and fry until golden on all sides. Drain.
In the same oil, add whole spices (bay, cardamom, clove, cinnamon); sauté briefly.
Whisk together curd, fennel powder, ginger powder, red chilli powder and salt.
Add the curd masala to the pan; cook on medium stirring until oil surfaces (5 min).
Add fried potatoes; coat well. Add ½ cup water and simmer 10 minutes covered.

name: Vegetable Tenga
blurb: Vegetable Tenga is Assam's signature sour curry, brightened with tomato and lemon — a palate-cleansing counterpoint to rich dals. Tenga means sour and is a compulsory part of the traditional Assamese thali, served toward the end of the meal.
tip: Add lemon juice only off the heat; boiling it can turn the broth bitter.
method: Heat mustard oil; add panch phoron and let it splutter.
Add green chilli and ginger; sauté briefly.
Add cubed raw papaya; stir to coat.
Add tomato and turmeric; cook 3 minutes.
Add lemon juice and a little water; cover and cook until papaya is just tender.
Season with salt; the broth should remain light and sour.

name: Rajma Chawal
blurb: Rajma Chawal is Delhi and Punjab's ultimate Sunday meal — rich, slow-cooked kidney beans over rice, a combination so beloved it has spawned restaurants, T-shirts and a generational nostalgia that transcends regional identity. Every Punjabi home has a slightly different rajma recipe.
tip: Cook rajma in its soaking water — the liquid carries flavour that is lost when you drain and start fresh.
method: Pressure cook soaked rajma until very tender (5–6 whistles); do not drain.
Cook basmati rice until fluffy; keep warm.
Heat oil; fry onion until deep brown. Add ginger-garlic paste; cook 2 min.
Add tomato and rajma masala; cook until oil surfaces.
Add cooked rajma with its liquid; simmer 20 minutes mashing a few beans.
Serve rajma over rice — they are always eaten together.

name: Nadru Yakhni
blurb: Nadru Yakhni is a Kashmiri Pandit delicacy — lotus stem cooked in a fragrant yoghurt-based sauce (yakhni) scented with fennel and cardamom. Yakhni gravies are among Kashmiri cuisine's most elegant preparations: pale, aromatic and built without any browning or caramelisation.
tip: Slice lotus stem into equal-thickness rounds so they cook evenly — thick pieces stay hard while thin ones overcook.
method: Heat mustard oil; add cloves and bay leaf; sauté briefly.
Add sliced lotus stem; fry 2 minutes until lightly coloured.
Whisk curd with fennel powder, ginger powder, cardamom and salt.
Add curd mixture to the lotus stem; stir and cook on medium heat 8 minutes.
Add ½ cup water; simmer until lotus stem is fully tender and sauce coats it.

name: Kashmiri Paneer Curry
blurb: Kashmiri Paneer Curry follows the Wazwan tradition of cooking without onion or tomato — the sourced curd does all the work, bloomed with fennel and ginger powder that are the twin pillars of Kashmiri spice. The result is a delicate, ivory-hued curry of great depth.
tip: Use full-fat paneer and full-fat curd; both low-fat versions tend to split in the sauce.
method: Heat mustard oil; add whole spices (cardamom, clove, cinnamon); sauté 30 seconds.
Whisk curd with fennel powder, ginger powder, Kashmiri chilli powder and salt.
Add paneer and half the curd mixture; cook on medium 5 minutes.
Add remaining curd mixture; simmer until oil separates from the sauce (10 min).
Adjust seasoning; serve with rice or sheermal.

name: Dhokar Dalna
blurb: Dhokar Dalna is one of Bengal's most ingenious vegetarian dishes — a lentil cake (dhokar) fried golden and then braised in a fragrant potato curry. The dhoka absorbs the gravy while retaining its firm, satisfying bite, making it a prized centrepiece of the Bengali thali.
tip: Cool the steamed dhoka completely before frying; warm dhoka crumbles in hot oil.
method: Soak chana dal; grind coarsely with ginger and green chilli.
Season with salt; steam in greased moulds or a flat pan until firm (15 min).
Cut into diamond shapes once cooled.
Shallow-fry the dhokar pieces in oil until golden on both sides.
Make a potato curry with tomato, turmeric, cumin and garam masala.
Add fried dhokar pieces to the curry; simmer 5 minutes and serve.

name: Begun Bhaja with Dal
blurb: Begun Bhaja with Dal is a simple Bengali pairing that elevates an everyday dinner — the smoky crust of the fried brinjal contrasts with the light, delicately spiced moong dal. Mustard oil is non-negotiable; it carries the dish's characteristic pungency.
tip: Salt the brinjal slices before frying to draw out moisture and prevent oil splatter.
method: Slice brinjal into thick rounds; salt and rest 10 minutes, then pat dry.
Heat mustard oil generously; fry brinjal slices until golden on both sides. Drain on paper.
In the same pan, cook moong dal with turmeric and water until soft.
Temper the dal with panch phoron in hot oil; add green chilli.
Serve fried brinjal alongside the dal — they are eaten together.

name: Kolhapuri Paneer
blurb: Kolhapuri cuisine is Maharashtra's most fiery school — Kolhapur in southern Maharashtra is famous for its fierce red chilli use and complex spice blends. Kolhapuri Paneer brings this heat to a rich, coconut-thickened gravy that is emphatically not for the mild palate.
tip: Kolhapuri masala varies by brand — taste before adding to judge heat level.
method: Heat oil; add onion and sauté until deep brown. Add ginger-garlic paste; cook 2 minutes.
Add tomato and cook until oil separates.
Add Kolhapuri masala, grated coconut and sesame seeds; sauté 2 minutes.
Add whisked curd; stir and simmer 5 minutes.
Add paneer cubes; coat with gravy and simmer 8 minutes covered.
Garnish with coriander and serve with bhakri or rice.

name: Shengdana Kadhi
blurb: Shengdana Kadhi is Maharashtra's peanut-enriched kadhi — distinctly different from Gujarati kadhi in its use of ground peanuts and absence of sweetness. It is a peasant dish from the Vidarbha and Marathwada regions where peanuts are a primary crop.
tip: Stir continuously after adding the curd mixture — any pause can cause it to split or stick.
ingredients: Peanuts — ¼ cup, roasted and ground
method: Whisk curd with besan and salt in a bowl until smooth.
Heat oil; add mustard seeds, curry leaves, green chilli and ginger.
Pour in the curd-besan mixture; stir continuously on low heat 8 minutes until thickened.
Add ground peanut paste; mix well and simmer 3 more minutes.
Add jaggery; stir and adjust consistency with water. Serve hot with rice or bhakri.

name: Panchkuta Sabzi
blurb: Panchkuta Sabzi is a celebration of Rajasthan's desert ingenuity — five wild, sun-dried plants (panchkuta means five ingredients) cooked together into an intensely flavoured dry sabzi. All five ingredients grow wild in the Thar Desert and were historically preserved through drying for year-round use.
tip: Cook completely dry — any moisture makes panchkuta heavy and dulls its sharp, concentrated flavour.
method: Drain soaked ker, sangri, kumatiya and gunda.
Heat ghee; add soaked gunda and kumatiya; fry 2 minutes.
Add ker and sangri; sauté on medium heat 3 minutes.
Add red chilli powder, coriander powder and amchur; mix well.
Cook covered on low heat 10 minutes. Season with salt.
Serve with bajra roti — this dish is deliberately dry.

name: Kathal Ghee Roast
blurb: Kathal Ghee Roast is Mangalore's vegetarian answer to the legendary ghee roast — a fiery, aromatic preparation of raw jackfruit in a red-chilli and ghee-based masala. The restaurant Shetty Lunch Home in Mangalore made ghee roast famous; the jackfruit version is now celebrated in its own right.
tip: Drain and pat jackfruit completely dry before frying; moisture prevents the charring that defines the dish.
method: Boil jackfruit until just tender; drain and pat dry.
Marinate with ghee roast masala, curd, salt and turmeric for 15 minutes.
Heat ghee in a wide pan; fry onion slices until deep golden brown.
Add marinated jackfruit and fry on high heat until edges char slightly.
Add tomato and cook until gravy is thick and coats the jackfruit.
Finish with more ghee and curry leaves; serve with neer dosa.

name: Jackfruit Gassi
blurb: Jackfruit Gassi is the pride of Konkani coastal cooking — a rich, deep-red curry built on a paste of roasted red chillies and coconut that is ground on a stone slab. Gassi (from the Tulu word for curry) is the essential preparation of Mangalorean cuisine.
tip: Roast the red chillies and coriander seeds dry before grinding — this deepens the gassi's colour and flavour.
ingredients: Raw jackfruit — 2 cups, boiled and cubed
method: Grind coconut, red chillies, coriander seeds, cumin and tamarind into a thick paste using a little water.
Heat oil; sauté onion until golden.
Add raw jackfruit and the ground masala paste; cook on medium heat 5 minutes.
Add 1 cup water; cover and simmer 20 minutes until jackfruit is fully cooked and masala is thick.
Adjust salt and serve with neer dosa or rice.

name: Khichdi with Gujarati Kadhi
blurb: Khichdi with Gujarati Kadhi is the definitive Gujarati comfort meal — the sweetened, tangy kadhi complements the bland, nourishing khichdi. Gujarati kadhi is notably sweeter than its Rajasthani cousin; jaggery is what makes the difference.
tip: Stir the kadhi continuously from the start; even one minute unattended can cause it to split.
method: Cook rice and moong dal together with turmeric until soft and mushy (khichdi).
Whisk curd with besan, jaggery and salt; add water to make a thin batter.
Heat ghee; add mustard seeds, curry leaves, ginger and green chilli.
Pour in the curd-besan mixture; stir continuously until it thickens (10 min).
Serve hot kadhi poured over khichdi — they are meant to be eaten together.

name: Mor Kuzhambu
blurb: Mor Kuzhambu is Tamil Nadu's curd-based curry — a cousin of Kerala's mor kuzhambu and Karnataka's majjige huli, all descended from the same ancient South Indian tradition of cooking vegetables in tempered, spiced curd. The coconut paste makes the Tamil version thicker and richer than its Kerala counterpart.
tip: Never let mor kuzhambu boil after adding curd — it splits into grainy curds and watery whey in seconds.
ingredients: Raw banana or colocasia — 1 cup, cubed and boiled
method: Blend coconut, green chilli, ginger and cumin to a fine paste.
Boil colocasia or raw banana until tender; keep aside.
Whisk the coconut paste into the curd with turmeric.
Temper coconut oil with mustard seeds and curry leaves; add to the curd paste.
Add cooked vegetable; warm gently on very low heat. Do not boil.
Serve with rice — the consistency should be like a thin curry.

name: Sindhi Kadhi
blurb: Sindhi Kadhi is unlike any other kadhi in India — instead of a curd base, it uses roasted besan (gram flour) as the thickening agent, making it suitable for those who do not eat curd. The roasting is essential; raw besan makes the kadhi taste floury and bitter.
tip: Roast the besan until it smells nutty and turns light brown — this is the most important step in the entire dish.
method: Dry-roast besan in a heavy pan on low heat, stirring continuously, until golden and fragrant (5 min). This removes rawness.
Add chopped tomato and drumstick pieces; cook 3 minutes.
Pour in 3 cups water; bring to a boil stirring to prevent lumps.
Add bhindi, potato and tamarind; simmer 20 minutes.
Temper with cumin seeds in hot oil; pour over kadhi. Adjust salt and consistency.

name: Dalma with Ghee
blurb: Dalma with Ghee is the evening version of Odisha's temple dal — richer, more nourishing, and deliberately simple. The ghee is not optional; it is the flavour. This is the kind of meal that Odia grandmothers make when they want to restore someone.
tip: Use good-quality ghee and add it at the end off the heat to preserve its aroma.
method: Pressure cook toor dal with turmeric until very soft.
Cook yam and pumpkin together in a pot with water, panch phoron and red chilli.
Add soft-cooked dal to the vegetables; stir gently.
Drizzle generously with ghee; add grated coconut and season with salt.
Serve hot — dalma with ghee is best when freshly made.

name: Chhena Poda
blurb: Chhena Poda (meaning burnt cheese) is Odisha's most distinctive sweet — fresh paneer baked with jaggery until the exterior caramelises to an almost bitter crust while the interior stays soft and custardy. It is said to be Lord Jagannath's favourite offering at Puri Temple.
tip: The dark, almost charred exterior is correct and intentional — do not remove it from the oven too early.
method: Crumble fresh chhena into a bowl; add jaggery, semolina, cardamom and mix well.
Fold in cashews and raisins. The mixture should be slightly sticky.
Grease a baking pan with ghee; spread the mixture 2–3 cm thick.
Bake at 180°C for 35–40 minutes until the top is deeply caramelised and a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool completely before cutting — the crust should be dark brown.

name: Pesarattu Upma
blurb: Pesarattu Upma is Andhra's beloved combo dish — a crisp moong crepe wrapped around lightly spiced semolina upma. The contrast of textures makes it a filling dinner that is lighter than it looks.
tip: Serve immediately; the crepe softens within minutes of plating.
ingredients: Semolina upma — 1 cup (semolina ½ cup, onion, green chilli, ginger, oil 1 tsp, salt)
method: Prepare semolina upma: sauté onion, green chilli, ginger in oil; add semolina, toast briefly, add 1 cup hot water and cook dry.
Blend soaked moong dal with ginger, chilli and salt into a thick batter.
Spread pesarattu batter on a hot griddle into a thin round.
Place a portion of hot upma in the centre; fold the crepe over it.
Cook until crisp on both sides. Serve with coconut chutney.

name: Jhal Muri
blurb: Jhal Muri is Kolkata's most democratic street food — vendors on Victoria Memorial lawns and Howrah Bridge approaches toss this spiced puffed rice in conical newspaper cones. The mustard oil is what separates genuine Jhal Muri from imitations.
tip: Toss and eat immediately; even 5 minutes of waiting makes the puffed rice lose its crunch.
method: Boil potato until tender; cool and dice small.
Combine puffed rice, diced potato, onion, tomato, cucumber and green chilli in a wide bowl.
Add tamarind chutney, mustard oil and salt; toss vigorously.
Top with sev and serve immediately — jhal muri goes soggy within 2 minutes.

name: Singara
blurb: Singara is West Bengal's version of the samosa — but more triangular, with a filling that is potato-forward rather than pea-heavy, and a crust that is thicker and flakier. Every neighbourhood's mishti dokan has its own singara recipe, and Bengalis are fiercely loyal to their local variety.
tip: The dough must be quite stiff — a soft dough absorbs too much oil and turns greasy.
method: Boil potato cubes until half done; cool.
Make dough: rub oil into maida, add salt and water to form a tight dough; rest 20 min.
Mix mashed potato filling with peas, ginger, green chilli, cumin and spices.
Roll dough into rounds; cut into halves; shape each half into a cone.
Fill with potato mixture; seal edges with a little water.
Deep-fry in medium oil until golden and crisp.

name: Dahi Vada
blurb: Dahi Vada (or Dahi Bhalla in the North) is one of India's most ancient snacks — urad dal fritters soaked in water to make them tender, then drowned in curd and chutney. The contrast of warm-cool, soft-crisp, sour-sweet makes it one of Indian cuisine's most complete sensory experiences.
tip: Soaking fried vadas in water (not curd directly) is the step that makes them soft — skip it and they stay dense.
method: Soak urad dal 2 hours; grind to a smooth, fluffy batter. Season with salt.
Drop tablespoons of batter into medium-hot oil; fry vadas until golden brown.
Soak fried vadas in warm water for 2 minutes; gently squeeze excess water out.
Whisk curd smooth; arrange vadas on a plate and pour curd over.
Top with tamarind chutney, green chutney, cumin powder and chilli powder.

name: Khakhra
blurb: Khakhra is Gujarat's iconic thin, crispy flatbread — traditionally made by Jain communities as a shelf-stable, oil-free snack. Unlike phulkas which puff and soften, khakhra is pressed flat and dried on the tawa until completely crisp. It can last weeks without refrigeration.
tip: The key is patience — cook on the lowest possible heat to dry the khakhra without burning it.
ingredients: Methi (fenugreek) leaves — ¼ cup, finely chopped
method: Mix whole wheat flour, methi leaves, red chilli powder, cumin, oil, salt and curd into a soft but not sticky dough.
Divide into balls; roll each into a thin round (thinner than paratha).
Cook on a dry tawa on low-medium heat, pressing firmly, until both sides are dry, spotted and crisp.
Khakhra must be fully dry — continue cooking on very low heat if needed.

name: Chevdo
blurb: Chevdo is Gujarat's beloved travel snack — a spiced, crunchy poha mix that keeps for weeks and accompanies every Gujarati road trip, train journey and tea time. Each household adds its own combination of nuts and dried fruit.
tip: The mix crisps only once fully cooled — do not judge it while hot.
method: Heat oil; add mustard seeds, curry leaves and red chilli powder.
Add thin poha and toss quickly so it coats evenly.
Add peanuts, cashews and raisins; toss on medium heat 3–4 minutes.
Add turmeric, sugar and salt; mix well.
Spread on a plate to cool completely before storing. It crisps as it cools.

name: Mirchi Vada
blurb: Mirchi Vada is Jodhpur's most iconic street food — a massive green chilli stuffed with spiced potato and encased in a thick besan batter, sold by roadside stalls outside Jodhpur's Sardar Market. The chilli's heat against the mild potato filling is its defining paradox.
tip: Remove all seeds from the chilli to control the heat level; the chilli itself provides enough flavour without the seeds.
method: Make the stuffing: combine mashed potato with coriander powder, amchur and salt.
Slit each large green chilli lengthwise and remove seeds.
Fill each chilli with potato stuffing.
Make a thick batter with besan, ginger and salt; dip stuffed chillies to coat.
Deep-fry in hot oil until batter is golden and crisp.
Drain and serve hot with tamarind chutney.

name: Dal Kachori
blurb: Dal Kachori is Jaipur's most famous street food — a crisp, flaky shell enclosing a spiced urad dal filling, sold at chai stalls from 6 AM. The Rawat Mishthan Bhandar's version near Ajmer Gate has been feeding Jaipuris for over 80 years.
tip: Fry on medium heat only; a high flame seals the outside before the kachori puffs properly.
method: Soak urad dal; blend to a smooth, thick paste with fennel, ginger and chilli.
Season with salt; the filling should be stiff.
Make a dough with maida, salt, and oil; rest 15 min.
Stuff filling into dough balls; roll into thick puris.
Deep-fry on medium heat until puffed and golden on both sides.
Serve hot with tamarind chutney.

name: Chakli
blurb: Chakli is Maharashtra and Karnataka's most beloved festival snack — a crisp, spiral-shaped savoury made from rice flour that is fried to a satisfying crunch. No Diwali faral (snack box) is complete without it; every family has its signature ratio of sesame to cumin.
tip: The dough must be soft enough to press without cracking — if it cracks, add a few drops of warm water.
method: Mix rice flour, besan, sesame seeds, cumin, chilli powder, salt and hot oil into a stiff dough using warm water.
Fill a chakli press with the dough and squeeze in spirals onto a plate.
Heat oil on medium; fry chaklis in batches until golden and crisp.
Drain on paper; cool completely before storing — they crisp further as they cool.

name: Karanji
blurb: Karanji is Maharashtra's Diwali favourite — a half-moon pastry with a sweet coconut-jaggery filling, similar to Goa's nevri and Andhra's kajjikayalu. In Maharashtra, Karanji symbolises abundance and is made in large batches and gifted to neighbours during the festival.
tip: Seal the edges well with water and press with a fork; any gap will cause the filling to leak out into the oil.
method: Knead maida with a little oil and salt into a firm dough; rest 20 min.
Toast coconut in a dry pan until lightly golden. Mix with jaggery, cardamom and poppy seeds.
Roll dough into thin circles; place filling on one half, fold and seal edges.
Deep-fry in medium oil until golden on both sides.
Drain and serve; they firm up as they cool.

name: Mathri
blurb: Mathri is North India's evergreen snack — a firm, crumbly, ajwain-flavoured biscuit that is the pantry staple of every Punjabi and Rajasthani household. Made in bulk for journeys, festivals and unexpected guests, mathri paired with pickle and chai is a universal North Indian afternoon ritual.
tip: Fry on low heat — mathri must dry out from the inside; high heat browns the outside while leaving a raw centre.
method: Mix maida, ajwain, cumin, black pepper, salt and oil into a firm dough using water.
Divide into small balls; roll into thick discs (thicker than puri, smaller than roti).
Deep-fry on low-medium heat until very light gold and crisp throughout.
Drain and cool completely — mathri firms up further as it cools.
Store in an airtight tin; keeps 2–3 weeks.

name: Chana Jor Garam
blurb: Chana Jor Garam is Rajasthan's street food classic — spiced whole chickpeas sold piping hot in railway stations and bazaars across North India. The name means simply hot puffed chickpeas; the spicing is designed to be eaten quickly on the move.
tip: Warm the boiled chickpeas before seasoning — cold chickpeas absorb spices poorly.
ingredients: White chickpeas — 1 cup, soaked and boiled
method: Boil chickpeas until tender; drain and cool.
Combine chickpeas, onion, green chilli and coriander in a bowl.
Add black salt, cumin powder, chaat masala and red chilli powder.
Squeeze lemon juice; toss vigorously until every chickpea is coated.
Serve immediately.

name: Roasted Makhana
blurb: Roasted Makhana is India's most ancient snack food — fox nuts (lotus seeds) were eaten by Vedic sages as a sattvic, fasting-appropriate food thousands of years ago. Light, crisp and protein-rich, they have made a significant comeback as a health snack in modern India.
tip: Keep the heat on medium throughout — high heat makes them hard without crisping; low heat makes them chewy.
method: Heat a wide heavy pan on medium; add ghee.
Add makhana and toss continuously for 5–7 minutes until they puff further and turn crisp.
Reduce heat; add rock salt, cumin powder, black pepper and chilli flakes.
Toss to coat evenly; serve immediately while warm, or cool completely for storage.

name: Moong Dal Chilla
blurb: Moong Dal Chilla is North India's protein-rich breakfast crepe — a more filling alternative to the vegetable omelette with none of the cholesterol. Widely adopted in health-conscious kitchens, it is also a traditional Rajasthani breakfast eaten with achar and curd.
tip: Keep the batter thick — a runny batter produces lacy crepes that are difficult to flip.
ingredients: Green moong dal — ½ cup, soaked
method: Soak moong dal; blend with a little water to a thick smooth batter.
Add ginger, green chilli, turmeric, cumin and onion; mix well.
Heat a griddle; pour a ladleful of batter and spread into a small thick circle.
Drizzle oil around edges; cook 3 minutes until the bottom is set.
Flip and cook 2 more minutes until golden on both sides.

name: Pazham Pori
blurb: Pazham Pori (banana fritter) is Kerala's most beloved evening snack — a golden, crisp batter sleeve around a sweet, soft plantain interior. No school tiffin box, no roadside tea stall, and no Onam feast is complete without it. The use of coconut oil gives it a distinctive aroma.
tip: Use very ripe plantain (yellow with black spots) for maximum sweetness; unripe plantain stays starchy and bland inside.
method: Mix maida, rice flour, turmeric, sugar and a pinch of salt with water into a thick, smooth batter.
Peel plantain and slice lengthwise into thin strips.
Dip each plantain strip into the batter to coat evenly.
Deep-fry in coconut oil on medium heat until golden and crisp.
Drain and serve hot with chai.

name: Mandakki Oggarane
blurb: Mandakki Oggarane is North Karnataka's street-side puffed rice snack — simpler and earthier than Mumbai's bhel, its flavour built from mustard oil, peanuts and curry leaves. In Hubli-Dharwad, vendors sell it from large baskets at bus stands, and it is eaten standing up.
tip: Use the freshest mandakki (puffed rice) you can find; stale puffed rice soaks up oil and goes limp.
method: Heat oil in a wide pan; add mustard seeds and curry leaves; let them pop.
Add peanuts and fry until just golden.
Add onion, tomato and green chilli; toss briefly.
Add turmeric and puffed rice; toss vigorously on high heat for 2 minutes.
Season with salt; serve immediately while still warm and crisp.

name: Arisa Pitha
blurb: Arisa Pitha is Odisha's festival sweet — a dense, jaggery-sweetened rice cake fried until dark and fragrant. Made for Raja Parba (the agricultural festival) and other Odia celebrations, each pitha is pressed with a distinctive pattern using a wooden block.
tip: Fry on medium-low heat — the outside must not brown before the inside cooks through.
ingredients: Rice — 1 cup, soaked and ground to paste
method: Soak and coarsely grind rice to a thick paste.
Dissolve jaggery in a little warm water; mix into the rice paste.
Add sesame seeds and cardamom; the batter should be thick enough to hold its shape.
Heat oil on medium; drop tablespoons of batter and flatten into rounds.
Fry slowly until deep brown and cooked through (5–6 min per side). Drain well.

name: Sprout Salad Chaat
blurb: Sprout Salad Chaat is the street-food version of a sprouted legume salad — simpler and quicker than the chaat stall's more elaborate bhel, but carrying the same bright, tangy spirit. The sprouts provide complete protein without any cooking.
tip: Use freshly sprouted legumes for crunch; over-sprouted legumes (sprouted more than 48 hours) become too soft for chaat.
method: Combine mixed sprouts, onion, tomato, cucumber and green chilli in a bowl.
Add lemon juice, chaat masala and coriander; season with salt.
Toss well and serve immediately as a snack.

name: Ribbon Pakoda
blurb: Ribbon Pakoda (also called ribbon murukku) is Tamil Nadu's Diwali snack — a flat, crisp strip of rice-besan dough that crunches like a wafer. Simpler to make than spiral murukku, it is often the first snack prepared in Diwali batch-cooking sessions because it requires no special moulds.
tip: Use a ribbon attachment with a single wide slit; a narrow slit produces strings rather than ribbons and they break in the oil.
method: Mix rice flour, besan, butter, sesame, cumin, chilli powder, hing and salt with warm water to form a stiff dough.
Fill a murukku press fitted with a ribbon (flat slit) attachment.
Press directly into hot oil in long strips.
Fry on medium heat until pale gold and very crisp.
Drain, cool and break into pieces for serving.

name: Kadboli
blurb: Kadboli is a less-known Maharashtrian Diwali snack — crispier and lighter than chakli, made with a mix of rice flour and besan. Each region has its own shape; the Konkan version is ring-shaped while the Vidarbha version is straight.
tip: Fry on medium heat — high heat browns them before the inside dries out, making them soft on the inside.
method: Mix rice flour, besan, sesame, ajwain, chilli powder and turmeric with hot oil; add warm water to form a stiff dough.
Press through a kadboli mould or a chakli press with a flat attachment into small rings or sticks.
Deep-fry in medium-hot oil until light gold and crisp.
Drain well and cool before storing.

name: Tulsi-Ginger Kadha
blurb: Tulsi-Ginger Kadha is India's most trusted household remedy — tulsi is Ayurveda's queen of herbs, revered as an adaptogen, anti-viral and expectorant. Combined with ginger and pepper, this kadha has been simmered on Indian stoves for thousands of years at the first sign of seasonal change.
tip: Use fresh tulsi whenever possible; the volatile eugenol in fresh leaves far exceeds dried.
method: Bring 250 ml water to a boil.
Add tulsi leaves, sliced ginger, black pepper and jaggery.
Simmer 8 minutes until the decoction turns deep amber.
Strain into a cup and sip warm.

name: Ashwagandha Warm Milk
blurb: Ashwagandha warm milk is an ancient Ayurvedic rasayana — a nightly adaptogenic drink that is said to reduce cortisol, ease nervous tension and promote deep sleep. Turmeric adds anti-inflammatory support.
tip: Drink 30 minutes before bed; black pepper is essential as it dramatically increases ashwagandha bioavailability.
method: Warm milk in a saucepan over low heat — do not boil.
Whisk in ashwagandha powder, turmeric and cardamom until fully dissolved.
Add a pinch of black pepper (aids absorption of ashwagandha).
Remove from heat; stir in honey once slightly cooled. Serve warm.

name: Giloy Kadha
blurb: Giloy Kadha is Ayurveda's premier immunity decoction. Tinospora cordifolia (giloy) is classified as a rasayana herb — one that rejuvenates tissues and builds natural resistance. Combined with tulsi and black pepper, this kadha became widely adopted during respiratory illness seasons.
tip: Do not use powdered giloy for kadha; the fresh or dried stem releases the bitter tikta compounds that carry its benefit.
ingredients: Giloy stem or giloy powder — 1 tsp
method: Combine giloy, ginger and tulsi in a small pot with 250 ml water.
Add black pepper and bring to a boil; simmer 10 minutes until reduced by a third.
Strain into a cup; add jaggery and stir.
Sip warm; best consumed morning or evening.

name: Triphala Water
blurb: Triphala is Ayurveda's most prescribed rasayana — a tri-fruit formulation of amalaki, bibhitaki and haritaki that collectively support digestion, detoxification and cellular rejuvenation. Used for over 2,000 years, it is considered a tridoshic balancer.
tip: Start with ¼ tsp and gradually increase to ½ tsp; a sudden full dose can cause loose stools in sensitive individuals.
method: Mix triphala powder with warm (not hot) water.
Add honey if desired and stir well.
Drink on an empty stomach first thing in the morning, or just before bed.

name: Brahmi Tea
blurb: Brahmi tea is Ayurveda's memory tonic — Bacopa monnieri has been used in Indian medicine for over 3,000 years to sharpen cognition, calm an anxious mind and support the nervous system. Traditionally consumed by students and scholars.
tip: Do not boil brahmi; high heat degrades its bacosides. Steep off the boil for best potency.
ingredients: Brahmi leaves or brahmi powder — 1 tsp
method: Bring 250 ml water to a boil; remove from heat.
Add brahmi leaves or powder and ginger; steep 5 minutes covered.
Strain into a cup.
Stir in lemon juice and honey once warm (not hot). Serve immediately.

name: Shatavari Milk
blurb: Shatavari milk is Ayurveda's premier feminine tonic — Asparagus racemosus is classified as a sattvic herb that nourishes ojas (vital essence), supports hormonal balance and is traditionally prescribed for women at all life stages, from menstruation to menopause.
tip: Warm rather than boil the milk to preserve shatavari's delicate saponins.
method: Warm milk on low heat; do not boil.
Whisk in shatavari powder, cardamom and jaggery until fully dissolved.
Add saffron strands; stir and let steep 2 minutes off the heat.
Serve warm — best consumed in the evening.

name: Mulethi Tea
blurb: Mulethi (liquorice root) tea is Ayurveda's throat and respiratory remedy — glycyrrhizin in liquorice soothes inflamed mucous membranes and has antiviral properties. Combined with tulsi and ginger, this kadha has been a household remedy across India for generations.
tip: Do not consume daily for more than 4 weeks; mulethi in high doses can affect blood pressure with prolonged use.
method: Bring 250 ml water to a gentle boil; add mulethi powder, ginger and tulsi.
Simmer 8 minutes on low; strain into a cup.
Add honey when warm (not hot) and sip slowly.

name: CCF Tea
blurb: CCF (Cumin-Coriander-Fennel) tea is Ayurveda's tridoshic digestive tonic — the three seeds together balance Vata, Pitta and Kapha. Widely prescribed by Ayurvedic practitioners for bloating, sluggish digestion and post-meal discomfort.
tip: Sip slowly and warm — gulping rapidly reduces its digestive benefit.
method: Combine cumin, coriander and fennel seeds in a small pot.
Pour 250 ml hot (not boiling) water over them and steep 5 minutes covered.
Strain into a cup.
Add honey if desired and sip slowly between meals.

name: Amla Juice
blurb: Amla juice is Ayurveda's most celebrated morning tonic — a single amla provides 20 times the vitamin C of an orange. Consumed on an empty stomach it is believed to kindle digestive fire and slow oxidative ageing.
tip: Drink within 5 minutes of juicing; add a pinch of black salt to reduce the astringency.
method: Grate fresh amla or blend with 2 tbsp water and strain to extract juice.
Combine amla juice with honey, ginger juice, black salt and 200 ml water.
Stir well and serve immediately — amla oxidises quickly once juiced.

name: Moringa Leaf Tea
blurb: Moringa leaf tea harnesses what Ayurveda calls shigru — a tree described as capable of curing 300 diseases. Moringa oleifera leaves contain all 9 essential amino acids, iron, calcium and potent antioxidants. The tea is a gentle way to absorb these nutrients.
tip: Dried moringa is milder than fresh; for the fresh version, steep for only 2 minutes to avoid bitterness.
method: Bring 250 ml water to a simmer; add dried moringa and ginger.
Steep off the heat for 5 minutes covered.
Strain into a cup; add lemon juice and honey when warm.
Sip slowly in the morning or before meals.

name: Methi Water
blurb: Methi water is one of Ayurveda's simplest fasting tonics — soaking fenugreek seeds overnight releases mucilaginous compounds and alkaloids (especially trigonelline) that lower fasting blood sugar and aid digestion. Widely prescribed as a morning ritual.
tip: Chew and swallow the soaked seeds for maximum fibre benefit; do not discard them.
method: Soak fenugreek seeds in 250 ml water overnight (8 hours minimum).
In the morning, strain seeds out or drink with seeds for additional fibre.
Add lemon juice and honey; stir and drink on an empty stomach.

name: Karela Juice
blurb: Karela juice is Ayurveda's bitter medicine — bitter gourd contains compounds that mimic insulin and support glucose metabolism. Consumed for centuries in diabetic households across India, it is one of the most studied plants in Ayurvedic pharmacology.
tip: Peel and deseed karela before juicing to reduce extreme bitterness without losing the active compounds.
ingredients: Bitter gourd (karela) — 1 small, peeled and chopped
method: Peel and roughly chop karela; blend with amla and ginger if using.
Add 200 ml water and blend smooth.
Strain through a fine-mesh strainer pressing the pulp.
Add black salt and serve immediately on an empty stomach.

name: Jamun Juice
blurb: Jamun juice is Ayurveda's blood-sugar regulating tonic — the dark Indian plum has been used for centuries to support pancreatic function. Its deep purple pigment (jamboline) is considered one of nature's most effective insulin sensitisers.
tip: Do not strain too finely — the pulp contains the fibre that slows sugar absorption.
method: Wash ripe jamun and remove seeds.
Blend jamun with mint leaves and 100 ml water until smooth.
Strain through a fine mesh if desired.
Add black salt and cumin powder; stir and serve chilled.

name: Hibiscus and Rose Petal Tea
blurb: Hibiscus and rose petal tea is an Ayurvedic Pitta-pacifying drink, cooling to the body and beautifying to the skin in classical texts. The deep ruby colour comes from anthocyanins in hibiscus — potent antioxidants that support cardiovascular health.
tip: Steep hibiscus off the boil; a rolling boil makes the tea tart and tannic.
method: Bring 250 ml water to a gentle simmer; do not boil hard.
Add hibiscus flowers, rose petals and cardamom; steep 5 minutes off the heat.
Strain into a cup.
Stir in honey and sip warm or allow to cool and serve chilled.

name: Arjuna Bark Tea
blurb: Arjuna bark tea is one of Ayurveda's heart tonics, derived from Terminalia arjuna, a tree revered in ancient texts for strengthening the cardiac muscle. It is traditionally consumed in the morning on a light stomach.
tip: Add honey only when the tea is warm, not boiling — high heat destroys its beneficial enzymes.
method: Combine arjuna bark powder with cinnamon, cardamom pod and milk in a small pot.
Bring to a gentle simmer and steep 8 minutes — do not boil hard.
Strain into a cup; add hot water to adjust strength.
Stir in honey once slightly cooled and serve warm.

name: Tomato-Pepper Rasam
blurb: Tomato-Pepper Rasam is Tamil Nadu's daily medicine — a thin, pungent broth drunk straight from a tumbler or poured over rice. Piperine in black pepper and lycopene in tomato make rasam nutritionally potent; in Tamil households, rasam is the first thing prepared when someone falls ill.
tip: Rasam must be thin enough to pour through a strainer — a thick rasam is sambar. Do not over-reduce.
method: Soak tamarind in ½ cup warm water; extract the pulp and strain.
Combine tamarind water with chopped tomato and 2 cups water; bring to a boil.
Crush black pepper and cumin together coarsely; add to the boiling rasam.
Add garlic; simmer 10 minutes until the raw tomato smell disappears.
Temper with ghee, mustard seeds and curry leaves; pour over rasam.
Finish with coriander. Rasam should be very thin and peppery — not thick.

name: Kollu Rasam
blurb: Kollu Rasam is Tamil cuisine's medicinal soup — horse gram (kollu) is uniquely thermogenic among Indian pulses, traditionally prescribed in Siddha medicine for weight management, kidney stones and respiratory conditions. In Tamil Nadu, it is eaten every week in winter.
tip: Use the horse gram cooking water — it carries the rasam's characteristic tannic depth that water cannot replicate.
ingredients: Horse gram (kollu) — ¼ cup, boiled and water reserved
method: Boil horse gram until tender; strain and reserve the cooking water.
Prepare tamarind extract; combine with tomato and the horse gram water.
Add black pepper, cumin and crushed garlic; bring to a boil. Simmer 8 minutes.
Temper with ghee, mustard seeds and curry leaves; pour over the rasam.
Finish with horse gram pieces; simmer 2 minutes. Serve piping hot.

name: Mulligatawny Soup
blurb: Mulligatawny Soup is a dish with a dual identity — born in colonial Madras as a British adaptation of Tamil pepper water (milagu tannir), it evolved into a rich, coconut-based meal in its own right. The name itself is a corruption of milagu tannir — pepper water.
tip: Blend raw rather than cooked — this produces a creamier soup without the slightly gluey texture of cooked-then-blended lentils.
method: Blend red lentils with onion, tomato, coconut milk, ginger, garlic and curry powder using a little water.
Heat coconut oil; pour in the blended mixture.
Simmer 20 minutes until the soup is thick and fragrant.
Add turmeric and salt; adjust consistency with water.
Serve hot in bowls with a swirl of coconut milk.

name: Tomato Shorba
blurb: Tomato Shorba is a Mughal-era soup, refined in the kitchens of Lucknow and Hyderabad's nawabs. The spice profile — cinnamon, cardamom and black pepper rather than chilli — reflects the Persian influence that characterises high Mughal cooking.
tip: Use overripe tomatoes for maximum sweetness; under-ripe tomatoes make the shorba sour and thin.
method: Blanch tomatoes in hot water for 2 minutes; peel and blend to a smooth puree.
Heat oil; add cinnamon and cardamom; sauté 30 seconds.
Add onion and ginger; cook until soft but not coloured.
Add tomato puree; simmer 15 minutes on low heat until the raw smell disappears.
Add black pepper and salt; add cream and stir.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot in bowls.

name: Dal Shorba
blurb: Dal Shorba is Mughal court cuisine's refined lentil soup — the word shorba comes from Arabic for broth. Where peasant dal is thick and filling, Mughal shorba is velvety and delicate, finished with aromatic whole spices that perfume rather than overpower.
tip: Strain the shorba after blending for a silky texture worthy of the Mughal table.
method: Bring 1.5 L water to boil; add red lentils, onion, tomato, ginger-garlic paste, bay leaf and cumin.
Simmer 20 minutes until dal is fully cooked and soft.
Blend smooth using a hand blender; strain if desired.
Return to heat; season with garam masala, lemon juice and salt.
Serve in cups; drizzle fresh cream if desired. Garnish with coriander.

name: Moong Dal Soup
blurb: Moong Dal Soup is India's most healing food — the first thing cooked for the sick, the elderly and new mothers across every region. Yellow moong dal is considered the most easily digestible pulse in Ayurveda, and its gentle warmth is understood as restorative rather than merely nourishing.
tip: Do not fully blend; a half-smooth consistency gives it body without becoming too heavy.
method: Wash moong dal; pressure cook or simmer with water and turmeric until very soft.
Heat ghee in a small pan; add cumin seeds; let them splutter.
Pour ghee tempering over the dal; add ginger.
Add lemon juice; season with salt.
Blend partially for a half-smooth texture; thin with water if needed.
Garnish with coriander and serve in a bowl.

name: Drumstick Soup
blurb: Drumstick Soup is South India's healing broth — moringa drumsticks are among the most nutrient-dense vegetables on earth, containing calcium, iron and all essential amino acids. This light soup is prescribed in South Indian households for recovery, lactation and as a general winter tonic.
tip: Extract maximum flavour by boiling drumstick pieces until they are completely soft and scrape the inside flesh into the broth.
method: Boil drumstick pieces with toor dal, tomato and turmeric until very soft.
Blend or mash; strain to extract a smooth, thin broth.
Heat oil; add cumin seeds, black pepper and garlic; sauté briefly.
Add drumstick broth; bring to a simmer. Season with salt.
Garnish with coriander and serve hot in cups.

name: Palak Soup
blurb: Palak Soup is a hospital kitchen staple that deserves better — when made with fresh spinach and a restrained hand on the cream, it is vibrant green, velvety and deeply nourishing. The blanching and immediate cooling is what preserves the colour.
tip: Use the cold-water shock after blanching — this is the only step that keeps the soup brilliantly green rather than olive-drab.
method: Blanch spinach leaves in hot water for 1 minute; drain and transfer immediately to cold water. Drain again.
Blend blanched spinach with garlic and ginger until completely smooth.
Heat butter; sauté onion until soft. Add spinach puree and simmer 5 minutes.
Add fresh cream, black pepper and nutmeg; stir and adjust salt.
Serve hot in bowls — do not reheat after adding cream.

name: Kaddu Shorba
blurb: Kaddu Shorba is Rajasthan's warming soup — a velvety pumpkin broth with a touch of jaggery or honey that echoes the Rajasthani preference for sweet-spice balance. Pumpkin (kaddu) is one of the few vegetables that grew reliably in the desert, making it a cornerstone of Rajasthani cooking.
tip: Roasting the pumpkin before blending adds a smoky depth; boiling gives a brighter, fresher flavour.
method: Blend cooked pumpkin with onion, ginger and a little water until smooth.
Heat ghee; add cinnamon and cardamom; sauté 30 seconds.
Add the pumpkin puree; simmer 10 minutes.
Add salt and honey; stir in cream.
Serve warm in bowls; the shorba should be lightly sweet and subtly spiced.

name: Majjige Huli
blurb: Majjige Huli is Karnataka's cooling curd curry — a gentle, coconut-thickened buttermilk dish that is the vegetarian counterpart to Kerala's mor kuzhambu. In coastal Karnataka it is served as a digestive at the end of a meal, its cooling properties prized in the hot coastal climate.
tip: Never boil once the curd is added — high heat will curdle it. Keep the flame on its lowest setting.
ingredients: Ash gourd or cucumber — 1 cup, cubed
method: Blend coconut, green chilli, ginger and cumin to a fine paste with a little water.
Boil ash gourd or cucumber in a little water with turmeric until just tender.
Whisk the coconut paste into the curd until smooth; add to the cooked vegetable.
Heat coconut oil; add mustard seeds and curry leaves; pour over the curry.
Warm gently — do not boil the curd base. Season and serve with rice.

name: Panchphala Bowl
blurb: Panchphala (five-fruit) bowl is an Ayurvedic tradition of combining fruits that collectively balance all three doshas. Each of the five fruits contributes a distinct rasa (taste): sweet, sour, astringent — making the bowl nutritionally and energetically complete.
tip: Use seasonal, fully ripe fruit; unripe fruit is harder to digest and energetically heavy in Ayurvedic tradition.
method: Wash and peel all five fruits; dice apple, banana and papaya into even cubes.
Combine all fruits in a wide bowl.
Add honey, cardamom powder and lemon juice.
Toss gently and serve within 20 minutes.

name: Papaya-Pomegranate Chaat
blurb: Papaya-Pomegranate Chaat is a modern Indian fruit bowl rooted in the chaat tradition — tart, sweet, peppery and fresh in a single spoonful. Papaya is a Pitta-reducing fruit in Ayurveda; pomegranate is its blood-building complement. Together they make a digestive powerhouse.
tip: Use deep-orange, ripe papaya — pale or greenish papaya lacks sweetness and stays starchy.
method: Cube and combine papaya and pomegranate seeds in a bowl.
Tear mint leaves and add.
Mix together chaat masala, black salt, lemon juice and honey in a small bowl.
Pour dressing over fruit; toss gently.
Serve within 20 minutes — papaya softens quickly once dressed.

name: Mango-Coconut Salad
blurb: This Kerala-inspired pairing of ripe mango and fresh coconut is rooted in the Sadya tradition of serving fresh fruit with grated coconut as a palate refresher. The addition of cardamom is a Kerala signature — the spice grows wild in the Western Ghats that border the state.
tip: Use Alphonso or Kerala's local Muvandan mango; semi-ripe mangoes carry the best balance of sweet and tart.
method: Peel and cube mango; combine with grated coconut and torn mint leaves.
Squeeze lime juice over; drizzle jaggery (softened or powdered).
Add cardamom powder; toss gently.
Serve immediately — best enjoyed fresh when mango is at room temperature.

name: Watermelon-Mint Bowl
blurb: Watermelon-Mint Bowl is India's summer answer — the combination of watermelon, lime and black salt is found in street stalls from Delhi to Mumbai as a cooling tonic on hot afternoons. Black salt (kala namak) is what separates this from a plain fruit bowl.
tip: Serve immediately after dressing — watermelon releases a lot of juice in minutes and the bowl becomes a diluted soup.
method: Cube watermelon into bite-sized pieces; remove seeds.
Tear mint leaves and add to watermelon.
Squeeze lime juice over; add black salt and chaat masala.
Toss gently and serve immediately — watermelon releases water quickly.

name: Banana-Date-Walnut Bowl
blurb: This no-cook bowl draws on Ayurveda's tradition of combining naturally sweet, grounding foods for morning nourishment. Banana and dates provide quick energy; walnuts add omega-3 fats that classical texts associate with brain clarity.
tip: Eat within 20 minutes of preparation — banana browns quickly and dates absorb moisture from the bowl.
method: Slice bananas into a bowl.
Chop dates and roughly crush walnuts.
Add all ingredients to the bowl: honey, cinnamon, cardamom.
Toss gently and serve immediately at room temperature.

name: Amla-Apple Salad
blurb: This Ayurvedic salad pairs the cooling sweetness of apple with the sharp, astringent amla — a combination that balances Pitta and Vata doshas. The ginger adds digestive warmth to make it suitable year-round.
tip: Do not prepare ahead; amla and apple both discolour and lose vitamin C quickly once cut.
method: Grate amla finely (discard the central pit).
Dice apple and toss immediately with lemon juice to prevent browning.
Combine amla, apple, grated ginger, honey and black salt in a bowl.
Garnish with coriander leaves and serve within 10 minutes.

name: Guava Chaat
blurb: Guava Chaat celebrates one of India's most beloved winter fruits — eaten with spices since ancient times as a digestive after meals. The combination of sweet-astringent guava with tangy chaat masala and chilli is a quintessential Indian sensory experience that balances all six tastes.
tip: Use slightly under-ripe guava for chaat — fully ripe guava is too soft and sweet to hold the spices.
method: Wash and cube guava into bite-sized pieces.
Toss with red chilli powder, black salt, cumin powder and chaat masala.
Squeeze lemon juice over; add torn mint leaves.
Toss again and serve immediately.

name: Custard Apple Bowl
blurb: Custard apple (sitaphal) is South India's autumn gift — intensely sweet, fragrant and grainy, available only for a few weeks. This simple bowl celebrates it at its peak, paired with banana and coconut milk in a South Indian tradition of combining local fruits with coconut.
tip: Taste before adding honey — a fully ripe custard apple is intensely sweet and may need none.
method: Scoop out custard apple pulp, removing all seeds.
Slice banana and toss with lemon juice to prevent browning.
Combine custard apple pulp, banana slices, coconut milk, honey and cardamom.
Stir gently — custard apple is fragile.
Serve immediately or chill briefly.

name: Chikoo-Coconut Bowl
blurb: Chikoo (sapodilla) is one of India's most underappreciated fruits — naturally caramel-sweet, with a grainy texture similar to a ripe pear. This bowl celebrates it simply with coconut and cardamom, a combination that appears in South Indian fruit preparations.
tip: Use fully ripe chikoo — it should feel soft when pressed gently; under-ripe chikoo is gritty and tasteless.
method: Peel and cube chikoo; combine with grated coconut and raisins.
Add cardamom powder, honey and lime juice.
Toss gently — chikoo is soft and breaks apart easily.
Serve immediately or chill briefly.

name: Mixed Berry with Tulsi
blurb: This berry bowl bridges Ayurvedic and modern nutrition — tulsi (holy basil) is an adaptogen that reduces cortisol, while the anthocyanin-rich berries fight oxidative stress. Black pepper is added in Ayurveda to enhance absorption of the herb's volatile oils.
tip: Tear tulsi rather than chopping — a blade oxidises the essential oils that carry its adaptogenic benefit.
method: Wash and hull strawberries; combine all berries in a wide bowl.
Tear tulsi leaves finely and add to the berries.
Drizzle honey, lemon juice and a pinch of black pepper.
Toss gently and serve within 15 minutes — tulsi wilts quickly.

name: Kachumber
blurb: Kachumber is India's simplest and most universal salad — three diced vegetables, lemon, cumin and coriander. It appears as a side across the entire subcontinent from Punjabi dhabas to Malabari homes. Its genius is its restraint.
tip: Dice all vegetables to the same size so every forkful contains all three — uneven cutting means you get one vegetable per bite.
method: Finely dice cucumber, tomato and onion into uniform small cubes.
Add green chilli and coriander; toss together.
Squeeze lemon juice; add cumin powder and salt.
Toss and serve immediately — kachumber is a fresh salad and deteriorates within an hour.

name: Sprout Chaat Salad
blurb: Sprout Chaat Salad combines two Indian traditions — the nutritional wisdom of sprouting pulses (which multiplies their protein and reduces anti-nutrients) and the flavour tradition of chaat. Every gram of sprouted moong or chana is significantly more bioavailable than the unsprouted pulse.
tip: Sprout at home for best nutrition: soak 8 hours, rinse and keep wrapped in a damp cloth for 12–24 hours.
method: Combine mixed sprouts, tomato, cucumber, onion and green chilli in a bowl.
Add chaat masala, lemon juice, coriander and salt.
Toss well; taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve immediately — sprout salads wilt within 30 minutes of dressing.

name: Beet-Peanut Salad
blurb: Beet-Peanut Salad is a Maharashtrian koshimbir — a class of quick, tempered salads that appear at every Marathi meal as a cooling counterpoint to spicy main dishes. The earthiness of beetroot and crunch of peanuts make it one of the most satisfying in this family of salads.
tip: Grate beetroot on the largest grater holes for texture; finely grated beetroot releases too much moisture and goes mushy.
method: Grate beetroot; heat oil with mustard seeds until they pop.
Add curry leaves and green chilli; sauté 30 seconds.
Add grated beetroot and turmeric; toss and cook 3 minutes.
Remove from heat; add grated coconut, roasted peanuts, lemon juice and coriander.
Toss well and serve at room temperature.

name: Carrot-Ginger-Sesame Salad
blurb: Carrot-Ginger-Sesame Salad is a pan-Indian recipe drawing on the tradition of grated vegetable salads (koshimbir, pachadi) found across the subcontinent. Sesame oil is an unusual addition that bridges the Indian and East Asian pantry — it works especially well with ginger and carrot.
tip: Grate on the coarser setting for texture; finely grated carrot releases water and makes the dressing thin.
method: Grate carrots into a wide bowl; add grated ginger.
In a small bowl whisk lemon juice, sesame oil and honey.
Pour dressing over carrots; add roasted sesame seeds and coriander.
Toss well and serve immediately or chill 10 minutes.

name: Cucumber-Yogurt Raita
blurb: Cucumber Yogurt Raita is India's universal cooling accompaniment — served at every meal from Kashmir to Kerala as a digestive buffer against spiced food. The act of squeezing cucumber before adding is essential; it prevents a watery raita that cannot hold its own.
tip: Squeeze the cucumber very well — a wet raita dilutes the curd and loses its creamy body.
method: Grate cucumber; squeeze out excess water firmly using your hands.
Beat curd until smooth.
Add squeezed cucumber, cumin powder, green chilli, mint, coriander and black salt.
Stir well; taste and adjust salt. Serve chilled.

name: Raw Papaya Salad
blurb: Raw papaya salad is a light, enzyme-rich dish popular across Assam and North-East India, eaten as a digestive side. The unripe papaya contains papain which aids protein digestion.
tip: Squeeze grated papaya in your fist to remove excess moisture before dressing so it stays crisp.
method: Grate raw papaya and carrot into a wide bowl.
Add green chilli, coriander and roasted peanuts.
Squeeze lemon juice, drizzle honey and season with salt.
Toss and rest 5 minutes before serving to let flavours meld.

name: Mooli Salad
blurb: Mooli Salad is Punjab's simplest digestive side — raw white radish with its own leaves, dressed only with lemon, mustard oil and salt. In North India this salad accompanies every winter meal; the mild bitterness of the leaves and the peppery crunch of the radish cut through rich dals and curries.
tip: Use the leaves — they contain more iron than the radish and are at their best when young and fresh.
ingredients: Mooli leaves — ½ cup, finely chopped
method: Grate mooli and the mooli leaves finely.
Add green chilli, coriander, lemon juice and a few drops of mustard oil.
Season with salt; toss well.
Serve immediately as a side salad — mooli leaves wilt quickly.

name: Corn-Capsicum Chaat
blurb: Corn Capsicum Chaat is India's street food tradition applied to sweet corn — a quick toss of boiled corn with raw vegetables, chaat masala and lemon that appears on roadside carts from Delhi to Bengaluru. Simple, bright and satisfying at any hour.
tip: Use boiled corn rather than canned for best texture; canned corn is too soft for chaat.
method: Boil sweet corn until just done; drain and cool slightly.
Combine corn, capsicum, onion and tomato in a bowl.
Add chaat masala, lemon juice, salt and coriander; toss well.
Serve immediately — best eaten within 30 minutes.

name: Cabbage-Coconut Poriyal
blurb: Cabbage-Coconut Poriyal is Tamil Nadu's quintessential dry side dish — a lightly cooked vegetable poriyal seasoned with mustard seeds and finished with fresh coconut. Every Tamil household has a repertoire of poriyals; this is often the first one taught to new cooks.
tip: Cook on high heat and keep stirring — slow cooking makes cabbage watery and loses the fresh texture.
method: Heat oil; add mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves and green chilli; let them splutter.
Add shredded cabbage and turmeric; stir-fry on high heat 3–4 minutes.
Reduce heat; cover and cook 5 minutes until cabbage is just tender.
Add fresh grated coconut; toss well. Season with salt.
Serve hot or at room temperature.

name: Nadru Lotus Root Salad
blurb: Nadru (lotus root) is Kashmir's most prized vegetable — a crunchy, starchy rhizome harvested from the Dal Lake by houseboat communities. In this salad form it appears light and cooling, far removed from its more famous fried avatar (nadru chips).
tip: Boil lotus root in water with a teaspoon of vinegar to keep it from turning grey.
ingredients: Lotus root (nadru) — 1 cup, thinly sliced and boiled
method: Thinly slice boiled lotus root; combine with diced cucumber and pomegranate seeds.
Whisk lemon juice, fennel seeds, black salt and regular salt in a small bowl.
Pour dressing over the salad; toss gently.
Garnish with coriander and serve immediately or chill 10 minutes.

name: Oats Upma with Mixed Vegetables
blurb: Rolled oats tempered with mustard seeds and cooked with colourful seasonal vegetables — a fibre-rich, iron-boosting twist on the classic upma.
tip: Dry-roast the oats for 2 minutes before cooking; it prevents the upma turning mushy and deepens the nutty flavour.
ingredients: Peas, fresh or frozen — ¼ cup
method: Dry-roast the oats in a non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until lightly golden; set aside.
Heat oil in the same pan; add mustard seeds and let them splutter.
Add urad dal and curry leaves; fry 30 seconds.
Add onion, green chilli, and ginger; cook until the onion softens, about 3 minutes.
Add carrot and peas; stir and cook 3 minutes.
Sprinkle in turmeric, then pour in 1½ cups water and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the roasted oats; cook, stirring frequently, 4–5 minutes until the upma comes together.
Finish with lemon juice, season with salt, garnish with coriander, and serve hot.

name: Overnight Oats with Chia and Fresh Berries
blurb: Rolled oats soaked overnight with protein-rich chia seeds, yogurt, and fresh berries — a no-cook breakfast built for soluble fibre and omega-3s.
tip: Swap dairy yogurt for coconut yogurt to keep it fully vegan; it works equally well and adds a subtle tropical note.
ingredients: Mixed berries (strawberry, blueberry, raspberry) — ½ cup
method: Combine oats, chia seeds, yogurt, milk, honey, and cardamom in a jar or bowl.
Stir well to break up any clumps of chia seeds.
Cover and refrigerate overnight, or for at least 6 hours.
In the morning, give it a good stir; add a splash of milk if you prefer a looser consistency.
Top with fresh berries and pumpkin seeds; serve chilled.

name: Ragi Cheela
blurb: Thin, crisp finger-millet pancakes spiced with cumin and green chilli — one of the richest plant sources of calcium and iron in Indian cooking.
tip: Letting the batter rest 5 minutes after mixing helps the ragi flour hydrate fully, giving you thinner and crisper cheelas.
method: In a bowl, combine ragi flour, onion, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, coriander, turmeric, and salt.
Add water gradually, whisking to form a smooth, pourable batter (consistency of crêpe batter).
Rest the batter 5 minutes.
Heat a non-stick tawa over medium-high heat; brush lightly with oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter and spread in a thin circle; drizzle a few drops of oil around the edges.
Cook 2–3 minutes until the edges lift; flip and cook 1 minute more.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or yogurt.

name: Oats-Moong Dal Chilla
blurb: Savoury pancakes made from soaked split green moong and rolled oats — high in plant protein, soluble fibre, and iron, with a satisfying bite.
tip: For best texture, grind the batter to a coarse consistency rather than silky-smooth; the oats give it pleasant body.
ingredients: Moong dal (split green gram), soaked 30 min — ½ cup
method: Drain the soaked moong dal; add to a blender with oats, green chilli, ginger, and ¼ cup water.
Blend to a coarse, pourable batter; transfer to a bowl.
Mix in onion, cumin seeds, coriander, turmeric, and salt.
Heat a non-stick tawa; brush with oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter and spread to a 15 cm circle.
Cook 2–3 minutes until golden underneath; flip and cook 1–2 minutes.
Serve with green chutney.

name: Dalia Upma
blurb: Broken wheat (dalia) cooked with aromatic tempering and mixed vegetables — a low-glycaemic, high-fibre breakfast that sustains energy throughout the morning.
tip: Toast the dalia in ghee for 2 minutes before adding water; it deepens the nutty flavour and prevents clumping.
ingredients: Mixed vegetables (carrot, peas, beans), chopped — ¾ cup
method: Heat ghee in a pressure cooker or saucepan; add mustard seeds and let them pop.
Add urad dal and curry leaves; fry 30 seconds.
Add onion, green chilli, and ginger; cook until softened.
Add the mixed vegetables and turmeric; stir 2 minutes.
Add the broken wheat and toast, stirring, for 2 minutes.
Pour in 1¼ cups water; season with salt.
Cover and cook until the water is absorbed and dalia is tender, about 8 minutes (or 2 whistles in a pressure cooker).
Fluff with a fork, garnish with coriander, and serve hot.

name: Ragi Porridge
blurb: Finger millet porridge sweetened lightly with jaggery and flavoured with cardamom — a deeply nourishing breakfast with exceptional calcium content.
tip: Whisk the ragi flour into cold milk first before heating; adding it to hot liquid causes lumps.
method: Whisk ragi flour into ½ cup cold milk until completely smooth with no lumps.
Pour the remaining 1 cup milk into a saucepan and bring to a gentle simmer.
Slowly pour in the ragi-milk mixture, stirring continuously.
Cook over low heat, stirring, 5–6 minutes until the porridge thickens.
Add jaggery and cardamom; stir until the jaggery dissolves.
Serve warm.

name: Ragi Idli
blurb: Steamed finger-millet idlis that bring ragi's exceptional calcium and iron to the classic South Indian breakfast — fluffy, wholesome, and deeply satisfying.
tip: Use a ratio of 1:3 ragi to urad dal for the fluffiest texture; full ragi batter tends to yield dense idlis.
ingredients: Urad dal (split black lentil), soaked 4 h — ¼ cup
method: Blend the soaked urad dal and poha with a little water to a fluffy, smooth batter.
Mix in the ragi flour; add water to achieve a thick dropping consistency.
Add salt, cover, and ferment overnight in a warm place.
Grease idli moulds; ladle batter into each mould.
Steam in an idli steamer for 10–12 minutes until a skewer comes out clean.
Allow to rest 2 minutes before un-moulding.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.

name: Bajra Cheela
blurb: Crisp pearl millet pancakes spiced with ajwain and coriander — a gluten-free, iron-rich breakfast from the heart of Rajasthan.
tip: Bajra batter is naturally thicker than wheat batter; add water until it just flows easily off the ladle.
method: Combine bajra flour, onion, green chilli, ginger, ajwain, coriander, turmeric, and salt in a bowl.
Add water gradually and whisk to a smooth, pourable batter.
Heat a non-stick tawa over medium heat; brush lightly with oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter and spread to a thin circle with the back of the ladle.
Cook 2–3 minutes until the surface looks dry and edges turn golden; drizzle a little oil around the edges.
Flip and cook 1–2 minutes more.
Serve with yogurt and green chutney.

name: Moong Dal Cheela
blurb: Thin, golden savoury pancakes made from blended soaked moong dal — high in folate, plant protein, and iron, with a naturally light texture.
tip: Adding a tablespoon of semolina to the batter gives the cheela a slightly crisp edge without thickening it too much.
ingredients: Moong dal (yellow split), soaked 2 h — ¾ cup
method: Drain the soaked moong dal; blend with green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, and 3 tbsp water to a smooth batter.
Stir in onion, coriander, turmeric, asafoetida, and salt.
Heat a non-stick tawa over medium-high heat; brush with oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter and spread to a thin circle.
Cook 2 minutes until the underside is golden; drizzle oil around edges.
Flip and cook 1 minute more.
Serve with mint chutney or sliced cucumber raita.

name: Oats-Moong Dal Dosa
blurb: Lacy, ferment-free dosas from soaked moong dal and rolled oats — ready same-day yet packed with soluble fibre, iron, and protein.
tip: The batter is naturally thin; do not add more flour to thicken it — a thin spread on the tawa gives the characteristic lacy, crisp dosa.
ingredients: Moong dal (yellow split), soaked 1 h — ½ cup
method: Drain the soaked moong dal; blend with oats, green chilli, ginger, cumin seeds, and enough water to make a thin, pourable batter.
Stir in curry leaves and salt; rest 5 minutes.
Heat a non-stick tawa over high heat; splash a few drops of water — it should sizzle away immediately.
Reduce heat to medium; pour a ladleful of batter and spread in a thin circle.
Drizzle oil around the edges; cook 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp.
Fold and serve with coconut chutney and sambar.

name: Masoor Dal with Tomato and Lemon
blurb: Red lentils simmered until silky, brightened with ripe tomatoes and finished with fresh lemon — one of the most bioavailable plant-iron dishes in the Indian kitchen.
tip: Adding lemon juice after cooking (not during) preserves vitamin C, which significantly boosts the absorption of non-haem iron from the lentils.
method: Rinse the masoor dal and add to a saucepan with 2½ cups water and turmeric.
Bring to a boil, skimming foam, then simmer 15 minutes until the dal is completely soft.
Heat oil in a separate pan; add cumin seeds and let them splutter.
Add onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger; cook 1 minute, then add tomatoes and red chilli powder.
Cook until tomatoes break down into a thick masala, about 5 minutes.
Pour the masala into the cooked dal; stir and simmer together 5 minutes.
Remove from heat; stir in lemon juice, season with salt, garnish with coriander, and serve with roti or rice.

name: Mixed Dal (Moong-Masoor)
blurb: Yellow moong and red masoor lentils cooked together — combining the digestibility of moong with the exceptional iron content of masoor in one comforting bowl.
tip: This dal thickens as it sits; add a splash of hot water when reheating and it comes back to the right consistency.
method: Rinse both dals together; add to a pressure cooker with 2 cups water, turmeric, and salt.
Cook for 3 whistles; let pressure release naturally.
Heat ghee in a pan; add cumin seeds and let them splutter.
Add onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add garlic, ginger, and spice powders; cook 1 minute.
Add tomato; cook until soft, about 4 minutes.
Pour the tadka into the cooked dal; stir well and simmer 5 minutes.
Finish with lemon juice and garnish with coriander.

name: Palak-Rajma Curry
blurb: Iron-rich kidney beans simmered in a vibrant spinach gravy — a powerhouse combination that delivers exceptional plant iron alongside vitamin C to maximise its absorption.
tip: Cooking the spinach purée briefly in the oil before adding rajma removes raw bitterness and deepens the green colour.
method: Pressure cook the soaked rajma with water and a pinch of salt for 5–6 whistles until completely tender; drain, reserving liquid.
Blanch spinach in boiling water 1 minute; drain and blend to a smooth purée.
Heat oil; add cumin seeds, then onion, and cook until golden.
Blend tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and green chilli into a paste; add to the pan.
Cook the masala until oil separates, about 8 minutes.
Add turmeric, coriander powder, and garam masala; cook 1 minute.
Add spinach purée; fry 3 minutes.
Add cooked rajma and enough reserved liquid for a medium-thick gravy; simmer 10 minutes.
Season with salt and serve with roti or brown rice.

name: Mixed Legume Curry (Rajma-Chana)
blurb: Kidney beans and chickpeas braised together in a rich, spiced tomato-onion gravy — two legumes that together provide an extraordinary hit of plant protein, iron, and fibre.
