tip: Cooking both legumes in the same pot saves time; chickpeas take slightly longer, so start them 10 minutes ahead if cooking separately.
ingredients: Kidney beans (rajma), soaked overnight — ½ cup
method: Pressure cook soaked rajma and chana together with water and a pinch of salt for 6–7 whistles until tender; drain, reserving liquid.
Heat oil; add cumin seeds and bay leaf.
Add onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger; cook 1 minute.
Add tomato purée and all spice powders; cook until oil rises to the surface, about 8 minutes.
Add the cooked legumes with 1 cup reserved liquid; stir well.
Simmer 12 minutes until the gravy thickens and coats the beans.
Garnish with coriander and serve with rice or roti.

name: Palak Dal (Toovar-Spinach)
blurb: Pigeon peas and fresh spinach cooked together into a wholesome dal — toovar's mild earthiness and spinach's iron-rich vividity make this a nutritional cornerstone of South Indian meals.
tip: Stir the spinach into the dal in the last 5 minutes only; prolonged cooking dulls the colour and reduces vitamin content.
method: Rinse toovar dal; pressure cook with 2 cups water and turmeric for 4 whistles until soft.
Mash the cooked dal lightly with the back of a spoon.
Heat oil in a saucepan; add mustard seeds and cumin seeds and let them splutter.
Add curry leaves, onion, and green chilli; cook until the onion softens.
Add garlic and tomato; cook until the tomato breaks down, about 5 minutes.
Add tamarind pulp and the mashed dal with enough water for a medium consistency.
Simmer 5 minutes, then stir in the spinach; cook 3–4 minutes until wilted.
Season with salt, garnish with coriander, and serve with rice.

name: Vegetable Barley Khichdi
blurb: Pearl barley and moong dal cooked one-pot with seasonal vegetables — barley's beta-glucan fibre actively lowers LDL cholesterol, making this khichdi a therapeutic one-bowl meal.
tip: Pearl barley needs more water than rice; use a 1:3 ratio (barley to water) to ensure it cooks through without going mushy.
ingredients: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, peas), chopped — 1 cup
method: Rinse barley and moong dal separately; soak barley in water for 30 minutes if time allows.
Heat ghee in a pressure cooker; add cumin seeds and bay leaf.
Add onion and ginger; cook until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add mixed vegetables, turmeric, and coriander powder; stir 2 minutes.
Add drained barley, moong dal, 2 cups water, and salt.
Pressure cook for 4 whistles; let pressure release naturally.
Stir gently, add a splash of water if needed for porridge-like consistency.
Finish with lemon juice and garnish with coriander.

name: Mushroom-Methi Stir-Fry
blurb: Button mushrooms and fresh fenugreek leaves sautéed with spices — one of the few Indian vegetable dishes that provides meaningful plant-source vitamin D, while methi adds iron and fibre.
tip: Don't crowd the pan when frying mushrooms; cook in one layer so they sear golden rather than steam and turn watery.
ingredients: Fresh methi (fenugreek leaves), stems removed — 1 cup
method: Heat oil in a wide pan over high heat; add cumin seeds.
Add onion and cook until it starts to colour, about 4 minutes.
Add garlic and green chilli; cook 30 seconds.
Add mushrooms in a single layer; cook without stirring for 2 minutes to get golden colour, then toss.
Add turmeric, coriander powder, and Kashmiri chilli; stir well.
Add methi leaves; cook, stirring, 3 minutes until the leaves wilt and most moisture evaporates.
Finish with lemon juice, season with salt, and serve as a dry subji with roti.

name: Moong Dal and Spinach Curry
blurb: Yellow moong dal and fresh spinach in a lightly spiced gravy — easily digestible, iron-dense, and ideal for anyone managing iron deficiency.
tip: Moong dal cooks quickly; avoid over-boiling or it turns gluey. Cook just until the dal is soft but the grains still hold their shape.
method: Cook moong dal with 2 cups water and turmeric until soft but not mushy, about 15 minutes.
Heat oil in a separate pan; add cumin seeds.
Add onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger; cook 1 minute.
Add tomato, coriander powder, chilli powder, and garam masala; cook until oil separates.
Add the cooked dal and mix well.
Stir in spinach; simmer 4 minutes until wilted.
Finish with lemon juice, season with salt, and serve with roti.

name: Masoor Dal Soup
blurb: A light, warming soup of red lentils with aromatic spices and bright lemon — fast to make, exceptionally iron-rich, and light enough as an evening meal on its own.
tip: For a silkier soup, blend half the cooked dal and stir back into the pot; this creates body without adding cream.
method: Heat oil in a saucepan; add cumin seeds and let them splutter.
Add onion and cook until softened, about 4 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger; cook 30 seconds.
Add tomato, turmeric, and chilli powder; cook until tomato softens.
Add rinsed masoor dal and water; bring to a boil.
Simmer uncovered 15 minutes until the dal has dissolved completely.
Blend half the soup for a creamier consistency if desired.
Stir in lemon juice, season with salt, garnish with coriander, and serve.

name: Moong Dal Khichdi with Brown Rice
blurb: The classic Ayurvedic one-pot meal — split moong and brown rice cooked together with turmeric and cumin into a healing, easily digested porridge.
tip: Brown rice needs a longer soak (30 min) and more water than white rice; the 1:2.5 ratio of rice to water gives the right soft texture for khichdi.
ingredients: Brown rice — ½ cup, soaked 30 min
method: Rinse soaked brown rice and moong dal together.
Heat ghee in a pressure cooker; add cumin seeds, bay leaf, and asafoetida.
Add onion and ginger; cook 2 minutes.
Add the rice-dal mixture, turmeric, 2½ cups water, and salt.
Pressure cook for 5 whistles; let pressure release naturally.
The khichdi should have a soft, porridge-like consistency; add hot water and stir if needed.
Garnish with coriander and serve with yogurt and pickle.

name: Palak-Toovar Dal
blurb: A South Indian-style spiced pigeon pea dal finished with fresh spinach — toovar's protein and spinach's iron-calcium richness come together in one satisfying bowl.
tip: Use tender baby spinach for this dal; it wilts faster and has a milder flavour than mature spinach, which can taste bitter in dal.
method: Pressure cook toovar dal with 2 cups water and turmeric until very soft; mash lightly.
Heat oil; add mustard seeds and dried red chilli; let them splutter.
Add cumin seeds and curry leaves; fry 20 seconds.
Add onion and cook until golden.
Add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Add tomato, coriander powder, and sambar powder; cook until masala is thick.
Add the mashed dal with water for desired consistency; simmer 5 minutes.
Stir in spinach; cook 3 minutes until wilted.
Finish with lemon juice and season with salt.

name: Chana Dal
blurb: Split Bengal gram cooked slow with whole spices and a vibrant tomato-onion base — chana dal is exceptionally high in protein and soluble fibre, with a naturally low glycaemic index.
tip: Chana dal holds its shape even after pressure cooking; if you prefer a smoother texture, cook for one extra whistle and mash lightly.
ingredients: Chana dal (split Bengal gram), soaked 1 h — 1 cup
method: Pressure cook drained chana dal with 2 cups water for 4 whistles until tender but not mushy.
Heat oil; add cumin seeds, cloves, and cinnamon; fry 30 seconds.
Add onion and cook until golden, about 7 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger; cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes and all spice powders; cook until oil separates, about 7 minutes.
Add the cooked chana dal with its liquid; stir and simmer 8 minutes.
Adjust consistency with water; finish with garam masala.
Garnish with coriander and serve with roti or rice.

name: Mixed Sprout Pulao
blurb: Freshly sprouted legumes cooked with brown rice and fragrant whole spices — sprouting dramatically increases bioavailable iron and vitamin C in the beans.
tip: Home-sprouting takes 24–36 hours but boosts iron and folate content significantly; rinse the sprouts twice daily to keep them fresh.
ingredients: Fresh mint and coriander — for garnish
method: Wash and soak brown rice 30 minutes; drain.
Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot; add cumin seeds, bay leaf, cloves, cinnamon, and cardamom.
Add onion and cook until golden.
Add ginger-garlic paste and green chilli; cook 1 minute.
Add tomato, turmeric, coriander powder, and garam masala; cook until masala thickens.
Add sprouts and rice; stir to coat in the masala.
Add 1¾ cups water and salt; bring to a boil.
Cover tightly and cook on low heat 20 minutes until rice is done and water absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes, then fluff gently. Garnish with mint and coriander.

name: Moong-Methi Dal
blurb: Yellow moong dal cooked with fresh fenugreek leaves — methi adds bitter depth, iron, and a compound linked to blood glucose regulation.
tip: If fresh methi is unavailable, use 2 tbsp dried kasuri methi; add it with the spices rather than at the end.
method: Cook moong dal with 2 cups water and turmeric until soft; set aside.
Heat oil; add cumin seeds and let them splutter.
Add onion and cook until golden.
Add garlic; cook 30 seconds.
Add tomato, chilli powder, and coriander powder; cook until oil separates.
Add cooked dal; stir and simmer 5 minutes, adjusting water for medium consistency.
Stir in the methi leaves; cook 4 minutes until tender.
Finish with lemon juice and salt.

name: Mushroom-Barley Khichdi
blurb: Pearl barley and yellow moong cooked one-pot with earthy button mushrooms — barley's beta-glucan lowers LDL cholesterol while mushrooms contribute rare plant-source vitamin D.
tip: Add the mushrooms after the initial pressure release so they remain plump and meaty rather than dissolving into the khichdi.
method: Rinse barley and moong dal; soak barley in cold water for 30 minutes.
Heat ghee in a pressure cooker; add cumin seeds and bay leaf.
Add onion, ginger, and garlic; cook 3 minutes.
Add drained barley and moong; stir to coat.
Add 2¼ cups water, turmeric, pepper, and salt; pressure cook 4 whistles.
Let pressure release naturally; open the lid and gently fold in the mushrooms.
Cover (without locking) and steam on low heat 5 minutes until mushrooms are cooked.
Stir, check seasoning, garnish with coriander, and serve hot.

name: Bajra Khichdi
blurb: Pearl millet and moong dal cooked into a warming khichdi — a winter staple from Rajasthan that is rich in iron, plant protein, and provides sustained warmth and energy.
tip: A small piece of jaggery added during cooking balances bajra's naturally robust, slightly bitter flavour beautifully.
ingredients: Bajra (pearl millet), soaked 30 min — ¾ cup
method: Drain soaked bajra; rinse moong dal.
Heat ghee in a pressure cooker; add cumin seeds.
Add onion and ginger; cook until softened.
Add bajra and moong dal; stir to combine.
Add 2½ cups water, turmeric, salt, and jaggery if using.
Pressure cook for 5–6 whistles until the bajra is completely soft.
Let pressure release; open and stir well — the khichdi should be soft and porridge-like.
Garnish with coriander and serve with ghee, yogurt, and green chutney.

name: Vegetable Barley Pulao
blurb: Pearl barley cooked pulao-style with fragrant spices and mixed vegetables — an elegant, cholesterol-friendly alternative to rice that looks and tastes like a feast.
tip: Barley absorbs flavour deeply; toast it in ghee for 2 minutes before adding water to unlock a rich, nutty aroma.
ingredients: Mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, peas, corn) — 1 cup
method: Rinse barley; soak in cold water 30 minutes then drain.
Heat ghee; add cumin seeds, bay leaf, cloves, cardamom, and cinnamon.
Add onion and cook until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add ginger-garlic paste; cook 1 minute.
Add mixed vegetables; stir 2 minutes.
Add barley and toast, stirring, 2 minutes.
Add 2½ cups water, turmeric, garam masala, and salt; bring to a boil.
Reduce heat; cover and cook 25 minutes until barley is tender and water absorbed.
Fluff gently, garnish with fresh herbs, and serve with raita.

name: Dalia-Vegetable Khichdi
blurb: Broken wheat and moong dal cooked together with a medley of seasonal vegetables — a lighter, lower-glycaemic cousin of rice khichdi that is high in fibre and easy to digest.
tip: This khichdi comes together very quickly compared to rice or barley — watch it closely after the second whistle to avoid over-cooking.
ingredients: Mixed vegetables (carrot, peas, potato), chopped — ¾ cup
method: Rinse dalia and moong dal together.
Heat ghee in a pressure cooker; add cumin seeds and bay leaf.
Add onion and ginger; cook 2 minutes.
Add mixed vegetables and turmeric; stir 1 minute.
Add the dalia-dal mixture and toast, stirring, 1 minute.
Add 2 cups water and salt; stir well.
Pressure cook for 2 whistles; let pressure release naturally.
Open, stir gently, add a splash of water if needed.
Finish with lemon juice and garnish with coriander.

name: Sambar Sadam
blurb: Rice cooked with toor dal, tamarind, and a medley of vegetables in the quintessential Tamil sambar — a complete one-pot lunch.
tip: Use small shallots for authentic sweetness. A generous squeeze of ghee on top elevates the flavour.
method: Pressure cook rice and dal together with 3 cups water until soft.
Soak tamarind in warm water, extract juice and set aside.
Sauté mustard seeds, curry leaves, and asafoetida in a deep pot.
Add onion, cook until translucent, then add tomatoes.
Add tamarind water, sambar powder, turmeric, and vegetables.
Simmer 15 min until vegetables are cooked and sambar thickens.
Stir in cooked rice-dal mixture, season and simmer 5 min.
Serve hot topped with a drizzle of ghee.

name: Puliyodarai
blurb: Tamarind rice — a tangy, spiced temple offering that doubles as the most beloved Tamil travel and tiffin box lunch.
tip: The pulikachal (tamarind paste) can be made ahead and stored for a week. Adjust chilli to taste.
method: Soak tamarind in 1 cup warm water, extract thick juice.
Heat gingelly oil, add mustard seeds, both dals, and dry chillies.
Add curry leaves and asafoetida, then pour in tamarind extract.
Add turmeric, salt, and cook on medium until the paste thickens.
Mix in roasted groundnuts and cook until oil separates.
Add this pulikachal to cooled rice, fold gently to coat evenly.
Serve at room temperature — this dish tastes best that way.

name: Thayir Sadam
blurb: Curd rice — the cooling finale to every Tamil meal and a complete lunch on its own. Creamy, tangy, and deeply comforting.
tip: Use slightly overcooked rice for best texture. Full-fat curd gives a richer result.
method: Mash warm cooked rice lightly with a fork.
Mix in milk and let it cool to room temperature.
Beat curd smooth and mix into the rice until creamy.
Heat ghee, add mustard seeds, red chilli, and curry leaves.
Pour tempering over the rice and mix.
Add ginger, green chilli, salt, and coriander.
Garnish with pomegranate seeds. Serve chilled or at room temperature.

name: Keerai Kootu
blurb: Spinach and chana dal simmered with coconut — a nourishing Tamil kootu that is best eaten with hot rice and a drizzle of ghee.
tip: Blanch the spinach just before adding to preserve colour. A kootu should be thick, not watery.
ingredients: Chana dal — ½ cup, soaked 30 min
method: Cook soaked chana dal until just tender. Set aside.
Grind coconut, cumin, and green chilli to a coarse paste.
Blanch spinach in boiling water for 2 min, drain and roughly chop.
Combine cooked dal, spinach, and coconut paste in a pan.
Add turmeric, salt, and simmer on low for 8 min until thick.
Prepare tempering: mustard seeds, urad dal, red chilli, curry leaves in coconut oil.
Pour tempering over the kootu and serve with rice.

name: Elumichai Sadam
blurb: Lemon rice — bright, citrusy, and ready in minutes. A Tamil staple for festive days and lunchboxes alike.
tip: Use day-old rice for the best texture — fresh rice turns sticky when mixed with lemon juice.
method: Heat gingelly oil, add mustard seeds, both dals, and cashews.
When dals turn golden, add green chilli, ginger, and curry leaves.
Add turmeric and sauté 30 seconds.
Add cooled rice and mix gently on low heat.
Remove from heat, squeeze in lemon juice, and toss well.
Add roasted groundnuts and coriander, season and serve.

name: Thengai Sadam
blurb: Coconut rice — fragrant, mildly sweet rice tossed with fresh coconut and spices. A temple offering and a celebration in every bite.
tip: Fresh coconut is non-negotiable for this dish. Dry coconut gives a flat flavour.
method: Heat coconut oil in a wide pan.
Add mustard seeds, both dals, red chilli, and curry leaves.
Add cashews and green chilli, sauté until golden.
Add grated coconut and toast for 2 min on medium heat.
Add cooked rice, salt, and toss gently until evenly coated.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

name: Vatha Kuzhambu
blurb: A bold, tangy tamarind-based Tamil curry cooked with sun-dried manathakkali or sundakkai — poured generously over rice for a deeply satisfying lunch.
tip: Gingelly oil is essential — it gives the authentic flavour. This curry actually tastes better the next day.
ingredients: Manathakkali or Sundakkai vathal (sun-dried berries) — 2 tbsp
method: Soak tamarind in 1½ cups warm water, extract juice.
Heat gingelly oil, fry vathal until it puffs and darkens slightly.
Add mustard seeds, toor dal, and curry leaves.
Pour in tamarind extract, add sambar powder, coriander powder, turmeric.
Simmer on medium for 15–20 min until the kuzhambu thickens.
Add jaggery and asafoetida, simmer 2 more min.
Serve with hot rice topped with a spoon of ghee.

name: Paruppu
blurb: Toor dal cooked Tamil style — lightly spiced, finished with ghee and asafoetida. The backbone of a complete Tamil lunch plate.
tip: This dal should be thicker than North Indian dal fry — almost like a soft paste poured over rice.
method: Pressure cook toor dal with tomatoes and green chilli until very soft.
Mash the dal until smooth and creamy.
Add turmeric, salt and simmer on low for 5 min.
Heat ghee, add cumin seeds, red chilli, asafoetida, and curry leaves.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the dal.
Serve over hot rice as the base of a Tamil lunch plate.

name: Idli with Sambar
blurb: Soft, steamed rice-and-lentil cakes served with piping hot sambar — the most iconic Tamil breakfast, eaten in homes and dhabas across the state every morning.
tip: Use the 3:1 rice-to-urad ratio. Well-fermented batter is the secret to airy idlis.
ingredients: For sambar: toor dal — ¼ cup
method: Grind soaked dal and fenugreek until fluffy. Grind rice to a slightly coarse batter.
Mix both, add salt, and ferment overnight.
Pour into greased idli moulds and steam for 10–12 min.
Meanwhile, cook toor dal with tomato and shallots until soft.
Add sambar powder, tamarind water, turmeric, and simmer 10 min.
Temper with mustard seeds and curry leaves.
Serve 4 idlis with a generous bowl of sambar.

name: Ven Pongal
blurb: Creamy, peppery rice-and-moong dal porridge — the quintessential Tamil breakfast offered in temples and eaten in millions of homes on weekends.
tip: The generous addition of ghee is not optional — it is what makes Pongal Pongal. Use good-quality peppercorns.
method: Dry roast moong dal until lightly golden.
Pressure cook rice and roasted dal with water and salt until very soft.
Mash until creamy — Pongal should be porridge-like.
Heat ghee, add cashews and toast golden.
Add cumin, pepper, ginger, curry leaves, and asafoetida.
Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the pongal and mix well.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.

name: Rava Upma
blurb: Semolina cooked with onions, green chillies, and curry leaves — a beloved South Indian breakfast that is ready in 15 minutes and keeps you full until noon.
tip: Roasting the rava until fragrant prevents lumps. Add water all at once and stir quickly.
method: Heat oil, add mustard seeds, both dals, and curry leaves.
Add onion, green chilli, ginger and sauté until onion softens.
Add tomato and cook 2 min.
Pour in boiling water, add salt, and bring to a boil.
Add roasted rava in a steady stream, stirring constantly.
Cover and cook on low for 3–4 min until water is absorbed.
Add lemon juice and coriander. Serve hot.

name: Adai
blurb: A thick, protein-rich lentil-and-rice crepe — earthier and more filling than a dosa. Made with mixed dals, eaten with jaggery or avial.
tip: No fermentation needed — just soak, grind, and cook. The batter should be coarser than dosa batter.
ingredients: Raw rice — ½ cup, soaked 2 hr
method: Grind soaked rice and dals with red chilli and ginger to a slightly coarse batter.
Add asafoetida, salt, and mix in curry leaves, onion, and coconut.
Heat a griddle, pour a ladleful and spread in a thick circle.
Drizzle oil around the edges, make a hole in the centre.
Cook until the base is crisp and golden, about 4 min.
Flip and cook the other side 2 min.
Serve with coconut chutney or jaggery.

name: Erissery
blurb: Pumpkin and black-eyed peas simmered in spiced coconut paste — a sweet-savoury Kerala curry that is as nourishing as it is comforting.
tip: The roasted coconut garnish at the end is not optional — it gives the dish its characteristic depth.
method: Cook pumpkin with turmeric, red chilli powder, and salt until just soft.
Add cooked black-eyed peas and mash a few pieces to thicken.
Grind coconut and cumin to a paste, add to the pan.
Simmer for 5 min until well combined.
In a separate pan, heat coconut oil and add remaining grated coconut.
Roast until golden brown, add mustard seeds, red chilli, curry leaves.
Pour the roasted coconut tempering over the erissery and serve.

name: Olan
blurb: Ash gourd and red cowpeas simmered in thin coconut milk — the most delicately flavoured dish on a Kerala sadya leaf, a study in restraint.
tip: Do not let the coconut milk boil after adding — gentle heat preserves its sweetness.
method: Cook ash gourd and green chilli in thin coconut milk until tender.
Add cooked red cowpeas and simmer 5 min.
Season with salt.
Add thick coconut milk and heat on very low flame — do not boil.
Drizzle coconut oil and add curry leaves.
Serve immediately as part of a rice plate.

name: Parippu Curry
blurb: Kerala-style moong dal in coconut milk — richer and sweeter than North Indian dal, it is the first item poured onto a banana leaf at any sadya.
tip: The second pour of coconut oil and curry leaves at the end is the defining step — do not skip it.
method: Cook moong dal with turmeric until very soft and mushy.
Blend smooth or mash well.
Add green chilli, salt, and simmer on low.
Pour in thick coconut milk and heat gently — do not boil.
Prepare tempering: shallots, mustard seeds, red chilli, curry leaves in coconut oil.
Pour sizzling tempering over the dal.
Serve immediately over rice.

name: Vegetarian Jollof Rice
blurb: The beloved West African party rice — long-grain rice cooked in a rich tomato-pepper sauce, smoky and vibrant. This vegetarian version loses nothing of the original spirit.
tip: The secret is the "party smoke" — high heat at the end lets the bottom crust slightly for that iconic flavour.
method: Blend tomatoes, peppers, scotch bonnet, and one onion together.
Heat oil in a heavy pot, fry the sliced onion until golden.
Add tomato paste and fry 3 min until darkened.
Add the blended tomato-pepper mixture and cook on high heat for 20 min until thick.
Add thyme, curry powder, bay leaves, salt, and stock. Bring to a boil.
Add washed rice, stir once, cover tightly.
Cook on low heat 25 min. Raise heat to high for 2 min at the end for the smoky crust.
Serve garnished with spring onions.

name: Ewa Riro
blurb: Nigerian stewed black-eyed peas simmered in a bold tomato-pepper sauce — rich, protein-packed, and eaten with rice, bread, or plantain for lunch.
tip: Start with canned beans for speed, or soak overnight. The longer the sauce fries, the deeper the flavour.
ingredients: Palm oil or neutral oil — 2 tbsp
method: Blend tomatoes, bell pepper, scotch bonnet together.
Heat oil in a pot, add onion and fry until translucent.
Add the blended pepper mixture and fry on medium-high heat for 15 min, stirring often.
Season with salt (and seasoning cube if using).
Add cooked beans and stir to coat in the sauce.
Simmer 10 min until the sauce clings to the beans.
Garnish with spring onions. Serve with rice or plantain.

name: Vegetarian Groundnut Soup
blurb: A rich, peanut-based West African soup thickened with groundnut paste and spiced with peppers — warming, filling, and endlessly satisfying over rice.
tip: Roast your own groundnuts and grind fresh for the best flavour. Adjust chilli to taste.
method: Blend tomatoes, onion, scotch bonnet, ginger, and garlic.
Heat oil in a pot and fry the blended mixture for 10 min until thick.
Add tomato paste and stir well.
Whisk groundnut paste with stock until smooth.
Pour groundnut mixture into the pot, add sweet potato.
Simmer 20 min until sweet potato is tender and soup is thick.
Stir in spinach and cook 2 min.
Serve over rice.

name: Sai Bhaji
blurb: A one-pot Sindhi stew of spinach, dal, and vegetables — humble, deeply nourishing, and a staple of every Sindhi household at lunch.
tip: The key is to cook everything together from the start — no separate steps. Everything melts into one harmonious dish.
method: Pressure cook chana dal, spinach, potato, tomato, onion, methi, green chilli with all spices and 1 cup water for 3 whistles.
Let pressure release naturally.
Mash everything together into a thick, homogeneous stew.
Heat oil in a pan, add ginger-garlic paste and sauté.
Add the mashed mixture and simmer for 10 min, adjusting consistency.
Serve over plain boiled rice with a wedge of lemon.

name: Dal Pakwan
blurb: Sindhi Sunday-morning ritual: crispy deep-fried wheat crisps served with chana dal and three chutneys — this is Sindhi soul food at its finest.
tip: The pakwan must be completely crisp — if it bends, fry longer. Soak the dal overnight for the smoothest texture.
ingredients: For pakwan: whole wheat flour — 1½ cup
Green chutney and tamarind chutney to serve
method: Boil soaked chana dal until just tender but holding its shape.
Temper with cumin, turmeric, red chilli, and amchur.
Mix wheat flour with cumin, ajwain, salt, and oil.
Add water to make a stiff dough. Rest 15 min.
Roll thin and cut into rounds or squares.
Deep fry on medium heat until crisp and golden.
Serve dal in a bowl with pakwan on the side and chutneys.

name: Gongura Pappu
blurb: Toor dal cooked with sour gongura (sorrel) leaves — the defining flavour of Andhra cuisine. Bold, tangy, and deeply satisfying with rice and ghee.
tip: Gongura provides natural tartness — no need for tamarind. Use more leaves for extra sourness.
method: Pressure cook toor dal with gongura leaves, tomato, green chilli, and turmeric.
Once cooked, mash and blend until smooth.
Heat ghee, fry garlic until golden, add mustard seeds, cumin, red chilli, and curry leaves.
Add asafoetida, pour tempering over the dal and mix.
Simmer 5 min and serve with hot rice and a drizzle of ghee.

name: Gutti Vankaya Curry
blurb: Baby brinjals stuffed with a fiery peanut-sesame masala and slow-cooked in their own steam — one of the most beloved Andhra lunch curries.
tip: Slit the brinjals deep but do not cut through. Freshly roasted and ground peanuts make all the difference.
method: Grind peanuts, sesame, coconut, red chilli, coriander, turmeric, tamarind, and salt to a coarse paste.
Slit each brinjal into 4 from the base, keeping the stem intact.
Stuff the masala paste into each brinjal.
Heat oil in a wide pan, add mustard seeds and curry leaves.
Add stuffed brinjals and arrange in a single layer.
Cover and cook on low, turning occasionally, for 20 min until soft.
Serve with Andhra rice and pappu.

name: Mulakkada Pappu
blurb: Drumstick dal — toor dal simmered with drumstick pieces in a gently spiced Andhra base. A weekday staple across every Andhra home.
tip: Cook drumstick separately if you prefer firmer pieces. The dal should be creamy and slightly thick.
method: Pressure cook dal with drumstick, tomato, green chilli, and turmeric.
Mash dal smooth while leaving drumstick intact.
Add red chilli powder, salt, and water if needed. Simmer 5 min.
Prepare tempering with ghee, mustard seeds, cumin, red chilli, curry leaves, asafoetida.
Pour tempering over dal and serve with Andhra rice and papad.

name: Jolada Rotti with Ennegai
blurb: Jowar (sorghum) flatbread paired with stuffed brinjal curry — a rustic North Karnataka lunch that is gluten-free, deeply satisfying, and rich in fibre.
tip: Jowar rotis need practice — knead with very hot water and roll with wet hands for best results.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, curry leaves for tempering
method: Mix jowar flour with salt, knead with very hot water into a pliable dough.
Make balls and pat into thick rounds using wet hands.
Cook on a dry griddle on medium heat, turning until brown spots appear.
For ennegai: mix peanuts, onion, chilli, coriander, jaggery, tamarind, salt.
Stuff brinjals, cook in oil until soft (15 min covered).
Serve rotti with ennegai and a side of yoghurt.

name: Saaru
blurb: Karnataka's beloved thin rasam-like soup — made with tomatoes, tamarind, and the fragrant saaru pudi. Poured generously over rice for a light, restorative lunch.
tip: Saaru should be watery, not thick — it is a soup to pour, not a curry. Drink any leftover straight from the bowl.
method: Cook tomatoes and dal in 2 cups water until dal is soft. Blend or mash.
Soak tamarind, extract juice.
Add tamarind water, saaru pudi, turmeric, jaggery, and salt.
Simmer for 10 min until fragrant.
Prepare tempering with ghee, mustard seeds, cumin, red chilli, curry leaves, asafoetida.
Add tempering to the saaru, garnish with coriander.
Serve over rice or drink as a soup.

name: Sheer Chai (Noon Chai)
blurb: Kashmiri pink tea — brewed with special gunpowder tea, baking soda, milk, and salt, topped with crushed almonds and sesame. A warming winter morning ritual in the Valley.
tip: The pink colour develops from the reaction between baking soda and the special tea leaves. Brew patiently for the deepest colour.
ingredients: Kashmiri Noon Chai leaves (or green tea) — 1 tsp
method: Boil tea leaves in water for 5 min.
Add baking soda and stir — the water turns red.
Add milk and cardamom, simmer 8 min until a deep pink develops.
Add salt (Noon Chai is traditionally salty — omit for a sweeter version).
Strain into cups.
Top with slivered almonds and toasted sesame.
Serve with Kashmiri bread (girda or lavasa).

name: Kashmiri Kehwa
blurb: Saffron-steeped green tea spiced with cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves — the aromatic essence of Kashmiri hospitality, drunk morning and evening.
tip: Brew on the lowest flame and never boil. The longer it steeps, the more fragrant it becomes.
method: Bring water to a simmer with cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves.
Add green tea leaves and steep on low heat 5 min.
Add saffron and honey if using.
Strain into cups.
Top with slivered almonds and walnuts.
Serve immediately.

name: Kashmiri Haakh
blurb: Collard greens or Kashmiri saag cooked simply with water, asafoetida, and dried red chilli — Kashmiri cooking at its most elemental. Eaten with rice at lunch and dinner.
tip: Do not overcook — the greens should retain some bite. The flavour relies entirely on simplicity.
ingredients: Haakh (collard greens or kale) — 3 cups, roughly chopped
method: Heat mustard oil to smoking point to mellow its sharpness.
Add dry red chilli and asafoetida — let them sizzle 10 seconds.
Add haakh greens and toss well.
Add water, cover, and cook on medium for 12 min.
Season with salt.
Serve with plain rice — this is traditionally a very simple preparation.

name: Aloo Pitika
blurb: Mashed potato with raw mustard oil, shallots, and green chillies — Assamese food at its most comforting. Simple but utterly addictive alongside dal and rice.
tip: Use good-quality cold-pressed mustard oil — the raw, pungent version. Do not heat it. That rawness is the whole point.
method: Mash potatoes while still warm.
Mix in raw mustard oil immediately — it binds into the warmth.
Add shallots, green chilli, coriander, and salt.
Mix well by hand — Assamese cooks traditionally mix with fingers.
Serve at room temperature alongside rice and dal.

name: Khar
blurb: Assam's unique alkaline preparation — raw papaya and moong dal simmered with khar (alkali from banana peel ash). A must-know dish to understand Assamese cuisine.
tip: Khar is the distinctive ingredient — filter banana peel ash water or use food-grade baking soda as a substitute (½ tsp). The taste is slightly soapy and entirely unique.
ingredients: Raw papaya — 1 cup, peeled and grated
Yellow moong dal — ¼ cup, soaked
Khar water — 3 tbsp (or ½ tsp baking soda in water)
method: Heat mustard oil, add cumin seeds and green chilli.
Add moong dal and sauté 2 min.
Add grated papaya and cook 5 min, stirring.
Pour khar water and ½ cup plain water.
Simmer covered for 15 min until papaya is soft.
Season lightly with salt.
Garnish with coriander. Serve with rice.

name: Steamed Rice
blurb: Plain boiled or steamed rice — the neutral, nourishing base that ties together every South Indian meal and most Indian meals across all regions.
tip: The absorption method gives consistent results: 1 cup rice to 1¾ cups water. Let it rest 5 min off heat before fluffing.
ingredients: Rice (short-grain or long-grain) — 1 cup, washed well
method: Wash rice in cold water 2–3 times until water runs clear.
Combine rice, water, and salt in a heavy pot. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat to the lowest setting, cover tightly.
Cook for 12 min — do not lift the lid.
Remove from heat and rest, covered, for 5 min.
Fluff gently with a fork and serve immediately alongside sambar, rasam, dal, or any curry.

name: Phulka
blurb: Thin, feather-light whole-wheat rotis puffed directly over an open flame — the lightest form of Indian flatbread, eaten from Gujarat to Bengal at every meal.
tip: Roll very thin (2 mm) and cook on the tawa first, then place directly on the flame to puff. The puffing means steam is trapped evenly — a sign of good dough and thin rolling.
ingredients: Water — approximately ½ cup, slightly warm
A few drops of oil for the dough
method: Mix flour and salt, add water gradually and knead into a soft, smooth dough.
Add a few drops of oil and knead 2 min more. Rest, covered, 20 min.
Divide into small equal balls (smaller than chapati).
Roll each ball into a very thin round (2 mm).
Cook on a hot dry tawa for 30 seconds until small bubbles appear.
Flip and cook 20 seconds.
Place directly over a medium flame — it will puff into a ball in seconds.
Remove with tongs, wrap in a clean cloth to keep soft.
Serve immediately with any dal, sabzi, or curd.

name: Plain Paratha
blurb: Layered whole-wheat flatbread cooked with a touch of ghee — flakier and more substantial than a phulka. The everyday bread of North India, equally at home at breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
tip: The layering technique (roll, fold, roll again) is what creates the flakiness. Do not press too hard — the layers need air between them.
ingredients: Ghee or oil — 1 tsp for the dough + 1 tsp per paratha for cooking
method: Mix flour and salt, knead into a soft dough with water and a little ghee.
Rest covered for 20 min.
Make medium balls. Roll each into a circle (5 inches).
Spread a little ghee on the surface, fold into a half-moon, spread ghee again, fold into a triangle.
Roll the triangle out again into a thicker flatbread.
Cook on a medium-hot tawa with ghee, pressing gently, until golden on both sides.
Serve with pickle, curd, or any curry.

name: Plain Curd
blurb: Fresh set curd — cooling, probiotic, and essential. Eaten alongside rice and curry in South India, with roti in North India, and as a simple meal-ender across every region.
tip: Full-fat milk gives the thickest, most flavourful curd. The setting temperature (40–45°C) is critical — too hot kills the culture, too cool prevents setting.
method: Heat milk until just warm to the touch (40–45°C) — not boiling.
Add the curd starter and stir gently.
Cover and leave undisturbed in a warm spot for 6–8 hours.
Once set, refrigerate for 2 hours before serving.
Serve as a side with rice, roti, or paratha.
Use as a base for raita, kadhi, or lassi.

name: Brown Rice
blurb: Whole-grain brown rice — slightly nutty, more fibre-rich, and with a lower glycaemic index than white rice. Excellent with sambar, rasam, dal, or any South Indian curry.
tip: Brown rice needs more water (1:2.5 ratio) and longer cooking. Soaking for 30 min before cooking speeds it up and improves texture.
ingredients: Brown rice — 1 cup, soaked 30 min and washed
method: Drain soaked brown rice and add to a pot with water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest heat.
Cover tightly and cook for 20–22 min.
Rest, covered, for 5 min off heat.
Fluff gently and serve with any curry, sambar, or dal.

name: Jowar Roti
blurb: Sorghum flatbread — gluten-free, fibre-rich, and a daily staple in rural Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan. Eaten with chutney at breakfast and with dal-sabzi at lunch or dinner.
tip: Jowar dough needs very hot water and quick work — it does not have gluten so it tears easily. Wetting your palms helps in patting it out.
method: Mix jowar flour and salt. Add boiling water gradually, mixing with a spoon.
Once cool enough to handle, knead into a smooth pliable dough.
Divide into balls. Wet your palms and pat each ball into a flat round directly on the tawa.
Or place between two sheets of wet plastic and roll gently.
Cook on a dry medium-hot tawa until small brown spots appear (2–3 min).
Flip and cook the other side.
Hold briefly over a flame for slight char and extra flavour.
Serve immediately with ghee, dal, or sabzi.

name: Bajra Roti
blurb: Pearl millet flatbread — warming, gluten-free, and a nutritional powerhouse. The winter staple of Rajasthan and Gujarat, eaten with ghee and garlic chutney.
tip: Like jowar, bajra needs hot water. The rotis are best eaten piping hot — they harden quickly as they cool.
method: Mix bajra flour and salt, add hot water gradually to make a pliable dough.
Knead well. Divide into equal balls.
Wet palms and pat each ball into a round directly on the tawa, or roll with wet plastic sheets.
Cook on a hot dry tawa, pressing gently with a cloth, until cooked through.
Hold over a direct flame briefly for slight char.
Serve hot with a generous knob of ghee.

name: Banana
blurb: The most widely eaten fruit across India — instant energy, rich in potassium, gentle on digestion. Eaten at breakfast, as a snack, or as an offering.
tip: Choose firm ripe bananas with small brown spots — they are sweetest at this stage.
method: Peel and eat as is.
Slice over porridge, oats, or poha.
Blend into smoothies or lassi.
Pair with a handful of nuts for a balanced snack.

name: Mango
blurb: The king of Indian fruits — sweet, fragrant, and bursting with vitamins A and C. Available through summer; a complete sensory experience eaten as is or with rice and ghee.
tip: Alphonso, Kesar, Dasheri, Langra — variety determines the flavour. Chill before cutting for the best experience.
method: Wash, peel, and slice the mango.
Eat fresh, or cube and serve in a bowl.
Traditional South Indian way: suck mango halves directly.
Can be paired with curd or rice for a complete summer meal.

name: Papaya
blurb: One of the most digestive-friendly fruits — rich in papain enzymes, beta-carotene, and vitamin C. Eaten fresh, with lime, or as a digestive starter to lunch.
tip: Press the skin gently — a ripe papaya yields slightly. Squeeze lime juice and a pinch of black salt for the classic Indian way to eat it.
method: Halve the papaya and scoop out seeds.
Peel and cut into cubes or slices.
Squeeze lime juice and sprinkle black salt.
Serve fresh as a first course or snack.

name: Guava
blurb: India's everyday superfruit — high in vitamin C, fibre, and folate. Eaten with a sprinkle of chaat masala and salt across street corners all over the country.
tip: Pick guavas with a slight yellow tinge — fully green ones are tart and hard, over-ripe ones are mushy.
method: Wash the guava well.
Quarter or slice it.
Sprinkle with chaat masala and salt in the classic Indian way.
Eat with or without seeds.

name: Pomegranate
blurb: Ruby-red arils bursting with iron, antioxidants, and vitamin K — particularly valuable for vegetarians. Eaten fresh, scattered over raita, or juiced.
tip: Roll the pomegranate firmly on a counter before cutting — it loosens the arils. Use a bowl of water to de-seed to avoid staining.
method: Score the pomegranate into quarters without cutting fully through.
Break apart over a bowl of water.
Separate arils by hand — the seeds sink, the pith floats.
Drain and serve fresh.
Optionally scatter over curd or use as a garnish.

name: Amla (Indian Gooseberry)
blurb: India's most potent fruit — amla contains 20× more vitamin C than an orange, is revered in Ayurveda, and is eaten raw, pickled, candied, or juiced.
tip: Raw amla is intensely sour and astringent — the bitterness fades quickly and leaves a sweet aftertaste. A pinch of salt brings out its flavour.
ingredients: Amla — 3–4 fresh (or 1 tbsp amla powder for off-season)
method: Wash fresh amla well.
Eat as is with a pinch of salt, or cut into wedges.
For amla juice: blend with water, strain, and add honey.
One amla daily in the morning is the Ayurvedic recommendation.

name: Watermelon
blurb: Summer's most hydrating fruit — 92% water, rich in lycopene and vitamin C. Eaten in thick slices on hot afternoons across India.
tip: Tap the watermelon — a deep hollow sound means it is ripe. Refrigerate whole for best flavour.
method: Cut watermelon into thick wedges or cubes.
Sprinkle black salt and lime if desired.
Serve ice cold.
Alternatively blend with mint for a fresh summer cooler.

name: Seasonal Fruit Bowl
blurb: A mix of seasonal Indian fruits — a nutritionally balanced start to the morning or a light afternoon snack that celebrates whatever the season brings.
tip: Use whatever is local and in season — a fruit bowl is most nutritious when the fruits have not travelled far.
method: Prepare all fruits and combine in a bowl.
Squeeze lime juice over the top.
Sprinkle chaat masala if using.
Garnish with mint leaves.
Serve immediately.

name: Kheer
blurb: Slow-cooked rice pudding simmered in full-fat milk with saffron, cardamom, and nuts — the quintessential Indian festive dessert.
tip: Cook on low heat and stir frequently — patience is the key to thick, creamy kheer. It thickens further as it cools.
ingredients: Saffron — a few strands, soaked in 1 tbsp warm milk
method: Bring milk to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pot.
Add washed rice, reduce heat to low.
Cook stirring frequently for 30–35 min until rice is very soft and milk thickens.
Add sugar and saffron milk, stir well.
Add cardamom, nuts, and rose water.
Serve warm or refrigerate and serve chilled.

name: Gajar Halwa
blurb: Slow-cooked grated carrot halwa — a winter festival favourite that fills the home with the aroma of ghee, cardamom, and khoya.
tip: Use Delhi red carrots for the authentic winter version — they are sweeter and more flavourful than orange carrots.
method: Heat ghee in a heavy pan, fry cashews and almonds until golden.
Add grated carrot and sauté on medium heat for 10 min.
Pour in milk and cook on medium, stirring often, until milk is absorbed (20 min).
Add sugar and khoya, mix well.
Cook until halwa leaves the sides of the pan.
Add cardamom and raisins.
Serve warm garnished with nuts.

name: Payasam
blurb: South India's kheer — semiya (vermicelli) or moong dal simmered in coconut milk and jaggery with cardamom. Every region has its own version; every sadya ends with it.
tip: Use thick coconut milk for the richest payasam. Add it only off the heat — boiling coconut milk can split.
method: Heat ghee, fry cashews until golden, add raisins.
Add vermicelli and toast until lightly browned.
Pour in thin coconut milk and simmer until vermicelli is soft (10 min).
Dissolve jaggery in 3 tbsp hot water, strain and add.
Simmer 5 min, then remove from heat.
Stir in thick coconut milk, cardamom, and saffron.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

name: Moong Dal Halwa
blurb: A labour of love — soaked yellow moong dal slow-roasted in ghee until golden, then cooked with sugar and milk. Rich, dense, and utterly indulgent.
tip: The roasting phase takes patience — at least 30 min on medium heat until the dal turns deep golden. Do not rush it or the halwa will be raw-tasting.
ingredients: Yellow moong dal — 1 cup, soaked 6 hr and blended coarse
Saffron — a few strands in 2 tbsp warm milk
method: Heat 4 tbsp ghee in a heavy pan. Add coarsely blended dal.
Roast on medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 30–35 min until deep golden.
Meanwhile, heat milk and dissolve sugar into it.
Add the sweet milk to the roasted dal gradually, stirring.
Cook until all liquid is absorbed and halwa comes together.
Add remaining ghee, cardamom, saffron milk, and nuts.
Serve warm.

name: Paal Kozhukattai
blurb: Rice flour dumplings simmered in sweet coconut milk with jaggery and cardamom — a comforting Tamil sweet eaten at festivals and on ordinary evenings alike.
tip: Make the rice flour balls small and even — they cook evenly and look more appealing. Do not boil after adding thick coconut milk.
method: Boil 1 cup water with a pinch of salt, add rice flour gradually, mixing.
Knead into a smooth dough. Shape into small marble-sized balls.
Cook rice balls in 2 cups boiling water until they float (5 min).
Dissolve jaggery in 3 tbsp water, strain.
Add jaggery water, coconut milk, and cardamom to the cooked balls.
Heat gently — do not boil.
Garnish with grated coconut. Serve warm.

name: Filter Kaapi
blurb: South Indian filter coffee — dark, fragrant decoction cut with hot milk and sugar, served frothed between two tumblers. The morning ritual of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Kerala.
tip: The froth (the trademark foam) comes from lifting the decoction high and pouring between tumbler and dabarah. Chicory blend is traditional and gives the signature bitter-sweet note.
ingredients: Filter coffee decoction — 4 tbsp (made with coffee-chicory blend in a filter)
method: Brew decoction in a traditional South Indian filter (upper vessel + lower vessel).
Heat milk until frothy.
Add 2 tbsp decoction to a tumbler.
Add hot milk and sugar.
Pour between the tumbler and the wide dabarah repeatedly to froth.
Serve in the tumbler with the dabarah on the side.

name: Neer Mor (Spiced Buttermilk)
blurb: Thin spiced buttermilk with ginger, green chilli, curry leaves, and asafoetida — the essential Tamil summer digestive, drunk at lunch and through the afternoon.
tip: Neer mor should be watery, not thick. The tempering in oil is optional but gives it a restaurant-style flavour.
method: Beat curd smooth, whisk in cold water until completely diluted.
Add ginger, salt, and asafoetida.
Bruise green chilli and curry leaves in your hand and drop in.
Mix in coriander.
Serve cold as a digestive alongside lunch or on its own.

name: Chaas (Spiced Buttermilk)
blurb: North Indian spiced lassi — thin, tangy buttermilk with roasted cumin, black salt, and ginger. The digestive drink of Rajasthan and Gujarat, drunk at every lunch.
tip: Use full-fat curd for a richer chaas. The roasted cumin powder is the backbone — freshly roast and grind for best flavour.
method: Whisk curd smooth with cold water until thin and frothy.
Add roasted cumin powder, black salt, regular salt, and ginger.
Add coriander and green chilli if using.
Stir well, taste for seasoning.
Serve cold over ice.

name: Plain Rice
blurb: Community recipe.
ingredients: 1 cup of raw rice - Sona Masoori, Surti Kolam, Govind Bhog, etc
method: 1. Wash and soak the rice for about 5 min in warm water.
2. Steam the rice 2 cups of water in pressure cooker - 3 or 4 whistles
3. Serve when hoy
Goes well as a staple food with most of the Indian dishes.
